And by the way, GUI Bloopers isn't just about bloopers.
It just uses them for contrast.

- Bob

> On Mar 1, 2015, at 6:18 AM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I've started creating issues on GitHub for your suggestions. GitHub issue tracking really is a great feature.
>
> Thanks for the book suggestions too! And good timing. I was just thinking the other day that I could use some new references on these topics. The only one I've heard of is The Pragmatic Programmer, but I haven't read it (only heard good things though). The others I'm not familiar with. I look forward to checking them out.
>
>
> On Fri, Feb 27, 2015 at 10:06 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Feb 28, 2015, at 12:36 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > ...
> > 4. The show/hide customization thing on the parameters plot
> > is hard to see.  I think we'll need conventions as to where
> > these general controls go.  For something this general, not
> > having it on the display itself makes sense to me if that's
> > possible.
> >
> > Yeah, I was trying to figure out where to put it and then I realized I was spending too much time fiddling with it so I just stuck it up there at the top right. But I agree that it's not great. What about sticking it up in the well panel to the right of the CI slider?
>
> That sounds good, though I might put it up front so
> it's in the same physical space on every page.  Maybe
> a small-ish button?  I don't know what kind of GUIs you
> use.
>
> By the way, I would highly recommend two books that changed
> the way I thought about GUI design (though I've read a lot of
> them):
>
>   * Jeff Johnson. GUI Bloopers.
>
> I read the first edition in book form and the second in
> draft form (the editor contacted me based on my enthusiastic
> Amazon feedback, which was mighty surprising).  I also like
>
>   * Stephen Krug.  Don't Make Me Think.
>
> I think I read the first edition and it's now up to the 3rd.  And
> also this one about general design:
>
>   * Robin Williams.  Non-Designers' Design Book.  (not web specific,
>       but great advice in general on layout)
>
> It's also many editions past where I first read it.  I'm also a huge
> fan of
>
>   * Hunt and Thomas.  The Pragmatic Programmer.
>
> for general programming and development advice (though you may be
> well beyond needing to read that --- we've implemented most of
> the recommended practices in Stan's workflow).
>
> If you want to buy them, I'm guessing Andrew won't mind reimbursing
> you (though you should ask first).  I keep giving away my own copies.
>
> > 5.  I didn't understand the "ALL theta_raw" vs. "theta_raw"
> > option, even after poking at it a bit.  "theta_raw" seems to
> > be a synonym for "theta[1]"?
> >
> > The way it should work is that if x is a vector (or matrix, etc) then "ALL x" will select all the elements so you don't have to add each of them individually. So "ALL theta_raw" should select all 8 of the theta_raw parameters. Is that not what's happening when you use it?
>
> I think it's the fact that you have "ALL theta_raw" and "theta_raw"
> as options --- it's really the second one that's confusing because
> it seems to be a synonym for "theta_raw[1]".
>
> > 6.  The greyed out names under the table don't seem to
> > work as controls, even thought they look like they'll be
> > editable because they pop up cursors.  I don't see the point
> > of having those.  I changed the 50% to "44%" and got "no records
> > found".  Then after I did that, nothing works at all.  So maybe
> > a "reset table" option would be helpful.
> >
> > Those controls show up automatically and I forgot to try to get rid of them. I just tried using them and, while they're not particularly useful, I haven't had the problem where everything stops working. Either way, I think I should just try to remove them.
>
> I agree.
>
> > 7.  I don't know what First/Previous/Next/Last are for.
> > They look like live buttons but can't be clicked.
> >
> > They should definitely be clickable in some cases. For example, if it's set to show 10 entries per page and you have 50 entries in the table you should be able to use those buttons to move between pages. But you won't be able to click "First" if you're on the first page or "Last" if you're on the last, etc. And you won't be able to click any of them if you're displaying all the entries on one page. Maybe there's a way to only have them show up under "clickable circumstances", so to speak.
>
> Or have them be clearly greyed out, which usually requires
> contrast with non-greyed-out elements.
>
> > 8.  In the search box, what am I supposed to be searching for?
> > It looks like I can enter parameters?  If I select "mu_raw"
> > and get just that, then edit the box on the bottom, it needs
> > to be one of the ones I'm viewing, which seems confusing.
> >
> > Yeah the search box is for parameter names, and you can use regular expressions. It's not always useful, but, for example if you have a lot of betas and a lot of sigma_betas then it's nice to be able to type ^beta and get only the betas without the sigma_betas. If I get rid of those boxes on the bottom will it be less confusing?
>
> Yes.  And maybe a label for "search parameters"?  But that's
> long enough you'd need to align it on top of rather than in
> front of the search box.  I'm not a huge fan of having text
> inside the box that goes away when you add your own.
>
> > 9.  What does the "Estimate" control at the top do?  It doesn't
> > seem to do anything when I click it, yet it looks like something
> > clickable.
> >
> > Oh, I can see why that's confusing. It's just the name for the tab that has the parameters plot and summary stats table (as opposed to the diagnostics, etc). I kind of like "Diagnose" and "Explore", so I went with "Estimate" the verb. But I could change it to "Estimates" or something else if anyone has a better idea.
>
> I actually figured that out when I went to other tabs and then
> went back.   I think it's OK as is.
>
> > 11.  The summary of sample parameters is fantastic.  Maybe an
> > option to include sd or intervals would make it even fantasticker.
> >
> > Well I definitely won't settle for fantastic when fantasticker is an option. Adding sds and/or intervals is definitely doable.
>
> The benefits of linguistics training.
>
>
> > 12.  How do you set the maximum lag for the correlation plots?
> > Oh, I see --- you've got customization for everything.  That's
> > really cool.  I still think the customization should be a bit more
> > front-and-center rather than in small text to the right.  Maybe
> > in the same control box as the one that lets you enter parameter names.
> >
> > That's how I used to have things, but for the plots with a lot of customization options (like the main parameters plot) the screen would get very cluttered. That's why I went with the separate panels that get transparent when you're not hovering over them. But maybe that's not the right solution.
>
> I'm not sure --- I would prefer something that was always in
> the same place and would pop up controls.  Hovering partial
> transparency usually confuses me (like in the default Mac terminal).
>
> > Thanks again for all the comment
> > Jonah
> >
> > P.S. Out of curiosity which web browser were you using? And were you using a laptop or trying it out on an iPad?
>
> I was using Safari on my Mac.  Everything worked just fine.
>
> I also have an iPad if you'd like me to try that.  We can probably
> get you one of those, too, if you don't have one and are going to
> be developing visualizations for it.  I could also try it on my iPhone.
> For that amount of money, we need to ask Andrew because it's coming out of
> his slush funds (our grants don't have any free money for books, computers,
> etc.)
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] expose Stan model user functions to interfaces (rstan)
messages.body_plain:
[moved to stan-dev]

> On Mar 3, 2015, at 3:06 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 6:16:27 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 10:39:25 PM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> >
> > It would still entail two compilations because the C++ source used to expose the user-defined functions is a shortened and heavily modified version of the C++ source used to draw from the posterior.
>
> Why does it need to be modified?  And how are you modifying it?

> 	• It ignores everything starting with the class definition for the model (because that isn't relevant to the user-defined functions)
> 	• It takes away the local namespace (because Rcpp can only expose functions from the global namespace), which entails cutting all the using:: statements from what used to be the local namespace and pasting them inside the user-defined functions (so as not to create conflicts in the global namespace)

That's really bad programming practice on Rcpp's part.
They probably did it for "simplicity".

One alternative would be to write global functions that call the namespace-based
ones.  Then you shouldn't need to modify the Stan-generated code at all, just
write a wrapper for it.

> 	• It gets rid of all the templating (because R can only use double or int)

Do you need to get rid of it?  Or is it just that it needs to only be instantiated
that way?  Again, calling from the outside should take care of this, too.

> 	• All the user-defined functions that end in _rng have their arguments rewired to not pass a RNG& (because Rcpp can't deal with it). Instead they get an int& seed = 0 argument and at the first line of the body of the function is inserted as static boost::ecuyer1988 base_rng__(seed);. Thus, that gets initialized once with the initial seed but has global scope.

Why can't Rcpp deal with a PRNG reference?  Is it just a problem
of passing in from R?  That is, there's no way to instantiate an RNG
in R?  Can't we do that by wrapping with Rcpp?

> 	• All the user-defined functions that end in _rng have their arguments rewired to not pass a T_lp_accum__& (because we can't template). Instead that is deleted and the first line of the body of the function is inserted as stan::math::accumulator<double> lp_accum__;.

I think this is problematic because it won't let you test the lp__ increments
inside the function.  Would it again be possible to call this from the outside?

> 	• All the user-defined functions have their arguments rewired to not pass a std::ostream* pstream__ (because Rcpp can't deal with it). Instead that is deleted and the first or second line of the body of the function is inserted as std::ostream* pstream__ = &Rcpp::Rcout;. Thus, if the user-defined function has print() statements, the Rcpp::Rcout thing makes sure they end up in R somehow.

Why not?  I have a feeling this is related to two questions back.

> 	• All the inline declarations get taken away for some reason I can't remember (probably a Rcpp limitation)

Is that just for the wrapper?  Again, calling from the outside would help
rather than modifying the existing function.  It's the modifications that
I think will be hard to maintain.

> 	• The relevant functions (but not their declarations if there are declarations) get marked with the attribute // [[Rcpp::export]] before their definitions

I don't even know what that means.  Is that a comment in
the C++ code that Rcpp can look at?

> 	• A variety of things get deleted from the corresponding functors. Perhaps the functors themselves should be deleted because I don't think they can be called from R anyway.

The functors are there because I need them to pass arguments
to the ODE solver.  Is it that they can't be called or that
Rcpp places restrictions on what can even be compiled?  I can't
imagine it's the latter or we'd never be able to call a Stan function.

> 	• Everything that looks like a templated type gets changed to a double, inclusive of all the internal const static bool propto__ = true; being changed to false so that (correct) log-density calculations will match those in R (if Stan is using the same parameterization)

That should be OK, but again I think it'd be better handled from
the outside.

> 	• There is some special handling of get_lp()
> 	• Dependencies are added to StanHeaders, BH, RcppEigen, and Rcpp so that it can find its #includes (because the compiler is not provided our ordinary CFLAGS)

> That's all. So, yes it probably will be a nightmere to maintain, but all of that was a result of it first failing to compile without it. So, if that is the price that we have to pay for users to be able to test their user-defined functions (and Sebastian can do his posterior predictive stuff outside of generated quantities) then so be it. It would be good to have a test .stan file with every conceivable kind of valid user-defined function (Sebastian got 90% of the way there by himself), so that Travis or something could alert us when it inevitably gets broken.

I'd rather take the approach of making things more modular.

> Ideally, as far as making something like this a feature that the other Stan interfaces could support, it would probably be better to have a flag that could be passed to stanc so that it would emit C++ code that would obviate the need for as many of the above tweaks as possible. But that would require a significant undertaking on the part of someone who understands stanc whereas my approach just requires a significant undertaking on the part of someone who understands regexes.

That's what I was hoping we could do.  It'd be pretty straightforward.

But I think it's going to be hard to coordinate this via Google+ or
e-mail, so maybe we can take it up more seriously when I get back and
you and Daniel and I can sit down in a room and go over it.

- Bob

They compile if you take away some of the extraneous arguments but I didn't know what they are for. Sebastian's file had some integrate_ode() stuff I think, so I guess it works at the moment.

Yes, I think having global wrapper functions is a good idea when you get back.

OK, so I've done the little dance to get line numbers
in and would appreciate both help and feedback at this
point.  Here's what I did in words:

for the model.  One holds the beginning and one the end
line of the next statement to be executed.  My first thought
was to make them member variables in the model class, but
that would prevent functions from updating them.

the statement class in the AST now holds a start and end
line.  (I could add column numbers or remove the last line.)
So now the model is peppered with assignments to these
statics.  (I hope that doesn't slow things down.)

made them members, but I should probably make them static.

Now what I can't figure out at least at first glance is where
the error messages are getting printed.  I looked through
services/command.hpp, which is where I suspected it would be,
but can only find a hard-coded output to std::cout for the
Newton optimizer.

I also saw that the "infomrational message" is cut-and-pasted
in two places in the code.  I'd like to try to get rid of this
duplication if possible.  But what I really want to know is
where the print's happening so that I can add the line numbers.

Thanks.

- Bob

parameters {

Running this generates this warning (note the first line!):

test that code was being generated properly in functions.

CmdStan, RStan, and PyStan easily, so any comments would be
greatly appreciated.

exchange to and from C++. For example, I'd love to figure out a way to

painful, IMHO.

looking at Protocol Buffers. (The new protocol buffers 3.0 also defines
a canonical serialization to JSON, which might be nice if one wants to
move away from rdump.)

and PyStan codebase by 30-40% by moving just about everything into Stan.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] how to output runtime error line numbers?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] how to output runtime error line numbers?
messages.body_plain:
First, THANK YOU BOB!  This has been a missing feature which has bugged me for ages.  I even made a few attempts at it but could never penetrate the parser far enough to figure out how to do it.

Anyway, would it maybe make sense to have the generated model code catch all exceptions and then update the message by including line numbers?  That way we don't have to update all callers that catch exceptions, just the model code.  Alternatively, we could have it catch exceptions and then rethrow a special Stan model exception which included the original exception plus this added information.  Then the variables that hold the line number information don't have to be member variables and can just be locals which may be faster.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Tue, Mar 3, 2015 at 9:00 AM Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> >> model::transform_inits catches and throws errors messages
> >> from exceptions thrown in io_writer, while model::log_prob
> >> throws exceptions while validating transformed parameters.
> >
> > But where are they caught and printed?  There aren't any
> > catches in the generated code for the model.
>
> services/init/initialize_state.hpp
>
> > Speaking of which, do you (Michael) want to rewrite this
> > message to suggest people look at n_divergent?  This is
> > the old message that tells them it's basically OK to
> > diverge.
>
> We have to be careful to separate out divergences from
> other exceptions, and I don’t think we do that carefully
> enough yet.
>
> > I see this in the main.cpp from cmdstan:
> >
> > int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
> >  try {
> >    return stan::services::command<stan_model>(argc,argv);
> >  } catch (const std::exception& e) {
> >    std::cerr << std::endl << "Exception: " << e.what() << std::endl;
> >    std::cerr << "Diagnostic information: " << std::endl << boost::diagnostic_information(e) << std::endl;
> >    return -1;
> >  }
> > }
> >
> > Does this catch ever get called?  I don't remember seeing exceptions
> > with diagnostic information, but I don't even know what that
> > boost call does.  I could wrap up stan::services::command
> > to catch and rethrow an exception that contains line
> > numbers (both programatically and in the what() return).
>
> Right now (at least in sampling) no exceptions should leak
> to that final catch.
>

messages.subject_clean: bug in v2.6.1; I'm undoing the tag.
messages.body_plain:
Since we haven't announced it to the world, I'm going to assume we can undo the tag without harm.

The long long pull request has stopped some of our matrix operations from working.

So that I could catch the RT.  That is, if I have
located_exception<out_of_range> and that uses the CRTP
to inherit from out_of_range, I should be able to catch
an out of range exception.  Of course, I'd then need to
cast down to located_exception<out_of_range>, which is
super ugly, so it's probably not much use.

Right now, we just brute-force handle all types of
exceptions the same way.  I guess we'll just have to
keep doing that going forward and I'll just just a single
located_exception with no templating and just have everything
be super generic with no way of finding the type of the
nested exception other than using run-time type info (RTTI).

- Bob

messages.subject: more on Win64 and var() actors
messages.subject_clean: more on Win64 and var() actors
messages.body_plain:
Ben inspired me to try again with ifdefs.  I'm optimistic the
current pull request will work with this:

#ifdef _WIN64
      // in WIN64, size_t = unsigned long long, which is a C++11
      // feature, so use this ctor to enable it
      var(size_t x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }
      var(ptrdiff_t x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }
#endif

The one that just failed was missing ptrdiff_t, which is the signed
type big enough to hold pointer differences.  On non-windows, this
is (long int);  on Windows, it's (long long int).

The built-in type ptrdiff_t is equal to (long long int) without
triggering C++11 warnings.   But we can't use it on anything but
Windows, because then there's ambiguity with (long int).

- Bob

P.S.  The bigger issue is that there are issues with the way we do arithmetic.
I think I'll try to fix that next as it should make a huge difference
in speed.  So should rewriting the way we do transforms with custom
(vectorized) derivatives.  And I'm also going to work on getting the
line-number errors in along the lines of Marcus's suggestions.

Alas, none of this is getting us closer to new features of the language,
just better speed and better error reporting.  For me, this is more
important than new features, but I should be available again for new
features in a few weeks once I knock off these two issues.

Now, off to do yet another talk on Stan in Sydney.  They love us here!

messages.subject: Re: Expose Stan functions to R
messages.body_plain:
I think we agree that if we can get by without (or with fewer regexps), then that would be good. But they work at the moment, so that is good enough for rstan. The next question is whether you can somehow make the entirety of the transformed parameters block, the model block, etc. into a function defined in the functions block so that you can then call it exactly in R?

Ben

On Wed, Mar 4, 2015 at 5:27 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> [is there a reason this isn't on stan-dev?]
>
> Sebastian's e-mail seems to missing the juicy bits.
>
> I would really rather not expose a pass-by-value vs. pass-by-reference
> distinction in Stan --- it's one of the things users find really
> confusing.
>
> Regexes are not the long-term solution here --- we need to either
>
>   1.  generate wrapper functions
>
>   2.  code generate what's needed inside language/generator.hpp
>
> Regexes are very very very brittle and will make it hard to put tests
> into Stan to make sure we don't break them on the R side.
>
> As a wise man (Jamie Zawinski apparently), once said,
>
>   If you have a problem and think regexes are the solution,
>   now you have two problems.
>
>   http://blog.codinghorror.com/regular-expressions-now-you-have-two-problems/
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Mar 5, 2015, at 2:54 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] more on Win64 and var() actors
messages.body_plain:
Nice, the unit tests passed and I'm optimistic the 6 hours of
distribution tests will pass if the unit tests passed (famous
last words if ever there were ones).

- Bob

> On Mar 5, 2015, at 9:22 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Ben inspired me to try again with ifdefs.  I'm optimistic the
> current pull request will work with this:
>
> #ifdef _WIN64
>      // in WIN64, size_t = unsigned long long, which is a C++11
>      // feature, so use this ctor to enable it
>      var(size_t x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }
>      var(ptrdiff_t x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }
> #endif
>
>
> The one that just failed was missing ptrdiff_t, which is the signed
> type big enough to hold pointer differences.  On non-windows, this
> is (long int);  on Windows, it's (long long int).
>
> The built-in type ptrdiff_t is equal to (long long int) without
> triggering C++11 warnings.   But we can't use it on anything but
> Windows, because then there's ambiguity with (long int).
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  The bigger issue is that there are issues with the way we do arithmetic.
> I think I'll try to fix that next as it should make a huge difference
> in speed.  So should rewriting the way we do transforms with custom
> (vectorized) derivatives.  And I'm also going to work on getting the
> line-number errors in along the lines of Marcus's suggestions.
>
> Alas, none of this is getting us closer to new features of the language,
> just better speed and better error reporting.  For me, this is more
> important than new features, but I should be available again for new
> features in a few weeks once I knock off these two issues.
>
> Now, off to do yet another talk on Stan in Sydney.  They love us here!
>

> On Mar 5, 2015, at 12:50 AM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:

> On 03/04, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>

...

>> Maybe efficiency isn't such a big deal, though.
>>
>
> If it's just the data for var_context (initialization and data) then
> this typically will not be that much data, especially if there was a
> binary serialization.

We've discussed binary formats before.  They'd be more efficient,
but they're a huge pain to maintain, doc, etc., and have the downside
that users can't inspect them by hand or with other programs without
a custom reader.   (Now if protocol buffers have a binary format, that
might help.)  There's also portability issues across 32-bit, 64-bit,
little endian and big endian, though I don't know how much of an issue

I'm still confused, so I'm probably missing the whole point of
this discussion.

Why would you need to wrap Eigen?  Can't you just
write C++ that just includes the Eigen lib?  Do we somehow need
to expose Eigen data structures to users?  For the same reason, I'm also
confused why RStan would need to use RcppEigen.

If you don't want to use Eigen, what would you like to use?
std::vector<std::vector<T>> is too cumbersome and many of our interfaces
are explicitly matrix based, which is why we chose to go with Eigen.
I agree that it's not the most portable thing in the world, which is
why I needed a lot of convincing to agree to going with Eigen.

> should also clarify that I mean going from a JSON serialized C++ class

I think that's pretty much impossible in general, since C++ classes
can be anything.   We could write specific cases if the data's all
strings or numbers.

> We've discussed binary formats before.  They'd be more efficient,
> but they're a huge pain to maintain, doc, etc., and have the downside
> that users can't inspect them by hand or with other programs without
> a custom reader.   (Now if protocol buffers have a binary format, that
> might help.)  There's also portability issues across 32-bit, 64-bit,
> little endian and big endian, though I don't know how much of an issue
> that is these days and if protocol buffers have binary formats, it's
> probably already solved for us.
>

Yes, binary and text (JSON in Protocol Buffers 3.0) serialization is
available. (As an aside, I'm not a huge fan of PB in general but for
dealing with C++ interop specifically it seems like the best tool.)

> ...

>
> > I actually don't have a good solution to this problem (that doesn't
> > involve wrapping Eigen). I could use help here. This is probably lower
> > hanging fruit than the command API refactor (but related).
>
> I'm still confused, so I'm probably missing the whole point of
> this discussion.
>
> Why would you need to wrap Eigen?  Can't you just
> write C++ that just includes the Eigen lib?  Do we somehow need
> to expose Eigen data structures to users?  For the same reason, I'm also
> confused why RStan would need to use RcppEigen.
>
> If you don't want to use Eigen, what would you like to use?
> std::vector<std::vector<T>> is too cumbersome and many of our interfaces
> are explicitly matrix based, which is why we chose to go with Eigen.
> I agree that it's not the most portable thing in the world, which is
> why I needed a lot of convincing to agree to going with Eigen.
>

Ok, I think we're on the same page here. Yes, I think the signature
should be std::vector<std::vector<T>> and that one should guarantee (not
hard, IIRC) that within each std::vector<T> memory is contiguous. I
*think* you can cast that to an Eigen matrix (in Stan). This would avoid
having Python or R touch Eigen.

> > should also clarify that I mean going from a JSON serialized C++ class
> > (or similar) to the C++ class itself --- that's what's (moderately)
> > painful.
>
> I think that's pretty much impossible in general, since C++ classes
> can be anything.   We could write specific cases if the data's all
> strings or numbers.

But in the specific case of var_context, Protocol Buffers could do it
easily. Remember what var_context is:

      std::map<std::string,
               std::pair<std::vector<double>,
                         std::vector<size_t> > > vars_r_;
      std::map<std::string,
               std::pair<std::vector<int>,
                         std::vector<size_t> > > vars_i_;
      std::vector<double> const empty_vec_r_;
      std::vector<int> const empty_vec_i_;
      std::vector<size_t> const empty_vec_ui_;

Serializing and deserializing (binary or text) is the sort of thing
Protocol Buffers was made for as far as I can tell.

Best wishes,

Allen

So we'd read the data out of the input stream, run the data

Where it'd create the transformed data internally in this second call?

Yes, we could start index fiddling with single arrays.
But it'd be easier to have a vector<vector<double>> interface.

We may wind up having to go to vector<vector<double>> anyway
when we start using ragged arrays for comparing chains of
different lengths.

I don't know what you mean by chains being too large
to serialize.  CmdStan writes them out to a file just
using ASCII, which is relatively slow, but not really
a bottleneck for Stan.

I wouldn't think that protocol buffers or JSON would replace
var_context --- they'd just be a way to get things into
memory.  What we need is not the memory underlying var_context
but the interface that lets us pull out values based on Stan
data types.  I'm sure we could implement that on top of JSON
or protocol buffers the same way it's now implemented on top of
our half-assed Rdump implementation (half assed in that it
doesn't support the same range of features as R itself, which
has a no-holds-barred approach to dump).

Michael and Daniel are working on refactoring the entire
interface.  So hopefully those 600 lines of code will be
reduced on both the RStan and PyStan sides.  It's just that so
many other issues keep coming up that neither of them have time
to work on it properly.

Thanks for doing the rundown of arguments.  You can see
something like that in the CmdStan manual, as well, because
I tried to doc it that way.

In the rundown of rstan::stan_args, the SEXP init_list is
the killer --- that's what we'd need something generic like
an in-memory structure for or would need to somehow marshal inside
of Python and R and pass in via memory.  That's where the
var_context comes in.  Serializing to and from JSON or protocol
buffers should be much much slower than staying in memory --- the
conversion back and forth from a character stream is very expensive.
As Marcus pointed out, this can dominate computation for some of
the efficient optimization models, like linear regression.

I have no idea what optim_alog_t is --- some kind of enum?

If we only ever deal with files in terms of their file names,
it should be easy --- I don't know if Daniel or Michael are
thinking along those lines or in terms of actual streams.

- Bob

Hi Ben,

QZ = Schur decomposition, right? This is a first step towards general evaluation of exp(A*t) to solve ODEs with constant A matrix.

The remaining bit as far is I recall is evaluating exp(T * t) with T being upper triangular - is this also in the making?

I need it for PK stuff - others for Markov systems. Would be awesome!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Stanbox!
messages.body_plain:
So I talked with Alan Edelman and he’s psyched about Stanbox.  He suggested we make a mockup—a Stanbox-looking object with a particular model that would help sell the concept.  What would be a good example?  8 schools seems too simple.  The pharmacology example is ok (if Novartis gives permission to use it) but maybe it’s too complicated? including other variants of the non-centered parameterizations.

need to trick the software into doing something, which has
seriously negative connotations (for me, at least)

OK, this must be my morning for ranting.

- Bob

Memory-wise it's a win over using a big model matrix but speed-wise it's not much of a win unless I >do gradients.

> a much smaller expression graph and hence much faster gradients

>
> Nice idea --- I hadn't even thought of doing something like that.
> Andrew (and to some extent the rest of us) thought people would
> be doing that with models.  Luckily, it hasn't been an issue.

Yeah, I don't know if it would be as helpful for people who haven't
been around as much Stan talk as me but the only things I knew going
in were conceptual.  I could see spending some time (in a month or
two) writing up the how-to for adding functions in detail.

>>  I think I'm going on the right path here but I thought I'd ask for feedback to make sure I'm not completely off the rails.
>
> The thing to do is to create a branch and check this in.
> We need to give you permission to do that on stan-dev.
> Can you send us your GitHub name?

Ok, I'd like to figure that process out. The github name is 'sakrejda'.

>
> Definitely on the right track, but I can rewrite it for you
> a bit. And you need to add doc in the usual Doxygen (Javadoc)
> format, but it's great you wrote what it did already.

The re-write's is awesome, I'll look at a diff to see what you changed exactly.

[snip/will do]

> The thing to do for efficiency is provide three var-based
> implementations that calculate partials as they go and then
> return a single var result.  This would be a huge speedup.

I realize you're juggling a lot of stuff but this is confusing, I need
you to throw me a bone here.  I get that this part is about the
gradients... My possibly-overlapping questions are:

1) why three implementations? what does Stan have three of here?
2) where do I look up what a var-based implementation is versus what
I've done so far (in the code is fine)
3) is there another .hpp file you can point to that has one of these
functions that calculates partials and returns one var?
4) is the gradient calculation a separate function, or is this just
modifying the present code?

Finally, there might be a different way of doing this that helps even
more.  I think Eigen probably has an efficient constructor for a CSC
format sparse matrix based on these vectors I'm passing into the
function (since that's how they store the matrix internally).  If I go
that route maybe it's possible to just use their sparse matrix
multiplication directly and define gradients for it that would get
re-used when you guys include sparse structures in Stan.  I guess that
wouldn't work if the efficient way to do it is to do the gradient at
the same time as the multiplication.

Krzysztof

>
> - Bob
>
>
> #ifndef STAN__MATH__MATRIX__SPARSE_MULTIPLY_HPP
> #define STAN__MATH__MATRIX__SPARSE_MULTIPLY_HPP
>
> #include <vector>
>
> #include <stan/math/matrix/Eigen.hpp>
>
> namespace stan {
>
>   namespace math {
>
>
>     /** Return the multiplication of the sparse matrix spefcified by
>      * by values and indexing by the specified dense vector.
>      *
>      * The sparse matrix X of dimension m by n is represented by the
>      * vector w (of values), the integer array v (containing one-based
>      * row index of each value), the integer array u (containing
>      * one-based indexes of where each column starts in w), and the
>      * integer array z (containing the number of non-zero entries in
>      * each column of w).
>      *
>      * @tparam T1 Type of sparse matrix entries.
>      * @tparam T2 Type of dense vector entries.
>      * @param m Rows in matrix.
>      * @param n Columns in matrix.
>      * @param v One-based row index of each value.
>      * @param u one-based index of where each column starts in w.
>      * @param z number of non-zer entries in each column of w.
>      * @return dense vector for the product.
>      * @throw ... explain error conditions briefly ...
>      */
>     template <typename T1, typename T2>
>     inline
>     Eigen::Matrix<typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1, T2>::type, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>
>     sparse_multiply(const int& m,
>                     const int& n,
>                     const Eigen::Matrix<T1, Eigen::Dynamic,1>& w,
>                     const std::vector<int>& v,
>                     const std::vector<int>& u,
>                     const std::vector<int>& z,
>                     const Eigen::Matrix<T2, Eigen::Dynamic,1>& b) {
>
>       // a whole bunch of error checking goes here, e.g., m, n > 0,
>       // etc. etc.  we can't throw index out of bounds exceptions at
>       // run time
>
>       typedef typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1, T2>::type fun_scalar_t;
>       Eigen::Matrix<fun_scalar_t, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>  y(m);
>       for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
>         int end = u[j] + z[j] - 1;
>         for (int q = u[j] - 1; q < end; ++q)
>           y(v[q]) += w[q] * b[j];
>       }
>       return y;
>     }
>
>
>   }
>
> }
>
> #endif
>

I prefer “implicit” or possibly “induced” but not “transformed” (i.e., my preference order is the reverse of Bob’s).  The trouble with “transformed” is that it sounds too mathematical:  you have a prior, then it gets transformed by a change of variables.  That’s mathematically correct but it hides the fact that, in many ways, the transformation is part of the prior (this is related to that 2004 paper of mine).

messages.body_plain:
> On Mar 7, 2015, at 12:45 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Fri, Mar 6, 2015 at 8:16 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>
>> The thing to do for efficiency is provide three var-based
>> implementations that calculate partials as they go and then
>> return a single var result.  This would be a huge speedup.
>
> I realize you're juggling a lot of stuff

Encouraging new contributors is very high on my priority list!

> but this is confusing, I need
> you to throw me a bone here.

src/stan/agrad/rev/functions/hypot.hpp

is the simplest non-trivial example of a function with two
potentially var inputs.  You can also look at

src/stan/agrad/rev/operators/operator_division.hpp

which is better because it's not symmetric so has all three
separate implementations.

Both of these have built-in C++ definitions, so you'd also need
the fourth signature which has everything instantatied with double
scalar values.

> I get that this part is about the
> gradients... My possibly-overlapping questions are:
>
> 1) why three implementations? what does Stan have three of here?

signatures  (var,double),  (double,var)  and (var,var), as well
as (double,double) here, but that doesn't need gradients.

> 2) where do I look up what a var-based implementation is versus what
> I've done so far (in the code is fine)

see above

> 3) is there another .hpp file you can point to that has one of these
> functions that calculates partials and returns one var?

see above

But you're going to be returning multiple vars.  But if
you look at our matrix functions, they're complicated by
memory management issues.

A good example to follow would be mulitply() of a matrix by
a vector.

> 4) is the gradient calculation a separate function, or is this just
> modifying the present code?

see the examples.

> Finally, there might be a different way of doing this that helps even
> more.  I think Eigen probably has an efficient constructor for a CSC
> format sparse matrix based on these vectors I'm passing into the
> function (since that's how they store the matrix internally).  If I go
> that route maybe it's possible to just use their sparse mat

> multiplication directly and define gradients for it that would get
> re-used when you guys include sparse structures in Stan.  I guess that
> wouldn't work if the efficient way to do it is to do the gradient at
> the same time as the multiplication.

Exactly.  You might want to use it for the stan/math version, and
even to produce the result value for the var version, but you need
to specify gradients to make it efficient.

It's OK to implement something with just templates without gradients
and then later make it faster.  We do that all the time.

- Bob

story.)

which is much less of a quagmire and which has a lot more wiggle room
for naming without confusing people.  But I'll stand by Stanbox being
confusing to anyone who knows what an Xbox is.  Now we could grab
a raspberry pi, give it to Ben, and get a Stanbox Mini back, or we

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
messages.body_plain:
The way I think of these, there are two models in play:

1.  The posterior we actually care about.

2.  The density over which HMC is actually performed.

If there are constrained parameters, Stan already provides
a built-in (implicit?) transform to some (2).  For example,
positive-constrained parameters are log transformed (with
Jacobian) to unconstrained ones.

Then we sometimes add additional (explicit?) transforms to ease
computation.  For example, applying the non-centered parameterization
to a hierarchical prior.

I take it the implicit or implied prior is the one we place
on (2) given that we want to be able to inverse transform
it back to (1).  Isn't that just going to be the original prior
times the absolute Jacobian determinant of the inverse transform?

I'm really not arguing about the terminology here, I just want
to understand it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
messages.body_plain:
This is basically the correct perspective.  Remember, that the posterior
is a probability _measure_, which is a parameterization-invariant, abstract
mathematical object.  The Stan Modeling Language defines a
probability _density_, which is a non-unique, parameterization-dependent
function from R^{n} -> R.  What this means is that a given model can be
represented different ways in Stan, and different representations have
different computational performances.

There’s nothing implicit or explicit or whatnot going on.  It’s just the fundamental
ambiguity of trying to define measures via densities.

messages.subject: Juxtaposing (marginal) prior and posterior in shinyStan
messages.subject_clean: Juxtaposing (marginal) prior and posterior in shinyStan
messages.body_plain:
For shinyStan, it would be pretty easy to allow the user to select a prior distribution to add to the posterior density plot for individual parameters so they can view both simultaneously and compare.

Is there any reason not to add this functionality? (The only thing I can think of is that in some cases priors are specified jointly and it might require some work for the user to figure out the marginal prior. But I don't think that's really a reason to avoid offering this.)

Assuming people think this is a good idea, the question is whether to allow the user to input code for a density function or to offer the user a list of choices of distribution families (along with input boxes to enter parameter values). I'm leaning towards the latter option so that we can be sure that it works and people don't spend too much time trying to code their functions properly, etc. The downside to providing a list of choices is that it would be limited to whatever we offer, but I was thinking that, as a start, the following should be sufficient to cover most cases:

normal,
student t,
cauchy,
beta,
gamma (and inverse gamma),
exponential,
chi-sq (and inverse chi-sq)

Are there others that would be essential to include in the first go-around that I'm blanking on?

I've attached two screenshots of this might look like (roughly).

messages.body_plain:
My point from my 2004 paper (also the talk that Mike saw me give in London) is that, when the parameterization changes, the model can change too, because we tend to use certain natural classes of prior distributions.  Thus, it’s not _just_ that we have a fixed distribution that we want to sample from, with reparameterizations being computational aids.  In addition, once we reparameterize and add prior information, the model itself typically changes, often in useful ways.  That is, the Pinocchio Principle.

>> On Mar 8, 2015, at 8:42 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>> My point from my 2004 paper (also the talk that Mike saw me give in London) is that, when the parameterization changes, the model can change too, because we tend to use certain natural classes of prior distributions.  Thus, it’s not _just_ that we have a fixed distribution that we want to sample from, with reparameterizations being computational aids.  In addition, once we reparameterize and add prior information, the model itself typically changes, often in useful ways.  That is, the Pinocchio Principle.
>>
>>> On Mar 7, 2015, at 5:53 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> This is basically the correct perspective.  Remember, that the posterior
>>> is a probability _measure_, which is a parameterization-invariant, abstract
>>> mathematical object.  The Stan Modeling Language defines a
>>> probability _density_, which is a non-unique, parameterization-dependent
>>> function from R^{n} -> R.  What this means is that a given model can be
>>> represented different ways in Stan, and different representations have
>>> different computational performances.
>>>
>>> There’s nothing implicit or explicit or whatnot going on.  It’s just the fundamental
>>> ambiguity of trying to define measures via densities.
>>>
>>>> On Mar 7, 2015, at 9:13 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> The way I think of these, there are two models in play:
>>>>
>>>> 1.  The posterior we actually care about.
>>>>
>>>> 2.  The density over which HMC is actually performed.
>>>>
>>>> If there are constrained parameters, Stan already provides
>>>> a built-in (implicit?) transform to some (2).  For example,
>>>> positive-constrained parameters are log transformed (with
>>>> Jacobian) to unconstrained ones.
>>>>
>>>> Then we sometimes add additional (explicit?) transforms to ease
>>>> computation.  For example, applying the non-centered parameterization
>>>> to a hierarchical prior.
>>>>
>>>> I take it the implicit or implied prior is the one we place
>>>> on (2) given that we want to be able to inverse transform
>>>> it back to (1).  Isn't that just going to be the original prior
>>>> times the absolute Jacobian determinant of the inverse transform?
>>>>
>>>> I'm really not arguing about the terminology here, I just want
>>>> to understand it.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>
>>>>

>>>>>
>>>>> For what it's worth I like 'implicit', or 'implied' maybe. I think it gives the right intuition (as well as being an appropriate description mathematically).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Juxtaposing (marginal) prior and posterior in shinyStan
messages.body_plain:
The big problem I see is that it's very error prone
to specify things in two places and try to keep them in
synch.  People tend to experiment a lot with models.  For
R, you'd need to use our parameterizations to remove the
ambiguity there.

That list doesn't come close to covering the range of
priors people are using for Stan.  For example, it doesn't
cover the multivariate cases, pareto, dirichlet, or
uniform, just off the top of my head.  There are also all
the issues around applying these to constrained parameters
like simplexes, ordered vectors, Cholesky factors, etc.

- Bob

> On Mar 8, 2015, at 8:57 AM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> For shinyStan, it would be pretty easy to allow the user to select a prior distribution to add to the posterior density plot for individual parameters so they can view both simultaneously and compare.
>
> Is there any reason not to add this functionality? (The only thing I can think of is that in some cases priors are specified jointly and it might require some work for the user to figure out the marginal prior. But I don't think that's really a reason to avoid offering this.)
>
> Assuming people think this is a good idea, the question is whether to allow the user to input code for a density function or to offer the user a list of choices of distribution families (along with input boxes to enter parameter values). I'm leaning towards the latter option so that we can be sure that it works and people don't spend too much time trying to code their functions properly, etc. The downside to providing a list of choices is that it would be limited to whatever we offer, but I was thinking that, as a start, the following should be sufficient to cover most cases:
>
> normal,
> student t,
> cauchy,
> beta,
> gamma (and inverse gamma),
> exponential,
> chi-sq (and inverse chi-sq)
>
> Are there others that would be essential to include in the first go-around that I'm blanking on?
>
> I've attached two screenshots of this might look like (roughly).
>

messages.body_plain:
i.e. roughly what Marcus is suggesting, in Stan code, would amount to this in the case where the "sparse" matrix was lower-triangular

/**
 * Return a vector that is the product of a lower-triangular matrix and a vector
 * @param L lower-triangular matrix but not checked for lower-triangularness
 * @param x column vector
 * @return column vector equal to L * x
 */
vector lt_multiply_mv(matrix L, vector x) {
  vector[rows(L)] out;
  int K;
  K <- cols(L);
  if (K != rows(x)) reject("L and x are not conformable for multiplication");
  for (k in 1:rows(L)) {
    if(k < K) out[k] <- sub_row(L, 1, 1, k) * head(x, k);
    else      out[k] <- row(L,k) * x;
  }
  return out;
}

In your case, you just have to deal with the arbitrary pattern of non-zeros.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: feedback on line exception class design
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: feedback on line exception class design
messages.body_plain:
The template pattern is really nice, but I'm not convinced it's worth it if you're not going to catch std::runtime_error and throw line_number_exception<std::runtime_error>.  The reason is that the pattern suggests that you should be able to catch a line_number_exception<special_exception_type> but that's only going to work if the model catches special_exception_type  and rethrows appropriately.  I.E., reasonably expected behaviour from the pattern will not work as expected which seems like a bad idea.

I see two possibilities:
1. Identify a short list of the exceptions that our code can throw and catch and rethrow explicitly.  Make it a policy that any functions to be used in models can *only* throw those kinds of exceptions.
2. Make a generic model_exception class which derives from std::exception.  Provide all the convenient RTTI/polymorphism features as functions of model_exception for when people care about exactly which exception was thrown.  E.G., have a model_exception::is_runtime_error() and model_exception::get_runtime_error().  This is almost what you have right now in effect but without the convenience functions since people would have to catch line_number_exception<std::exception> and then use RTTI to do anything more sophisticated than get the error message and line number.

Cheers,
Marcus

We haven't really discussed whether we want this function
in Stan!  We have to be careful not to just keep adding
functions because they introduce maintenance overhead downstream,
complicate the manual and thus make existing functionality a bit harder
to use, etc.

The major thing that worries me about this one is backward
compatiblity --- we're going to eventually want to do sparse
matrices the "right" way with a built-in data type.  At that
point, we'd want to deprecate this (and related) functions.

Is that OK with everybody?

More below.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] plotting sampler parameters
messages.body_plain:
There's also stepsize, but that only changes after adaptation
if the stepsize jitter parameter's set, which we don't usually
recommend.

So plot vs. iteration is just like a traceplot, right?  Treating
them like parameters makes sense to me.

The types matter:

* accept_stat is continuous
* treedepth is an integer
* n_divergent is binary (at least for NUTS and HMC)

Ideally, we'd use bar plots rather than histograms for discrete
quantities.   We can have discrete "parameters" produced as generated
quantities.  Right now, our print and plotting doesn't really do right
by these.

I'm not so keen on rug plots if that's the thing that prints the
observations on the horizontal axis as ticks and then plots
a density estimate above it.  And it won't work for n_divergent, because
it's a binary quantity.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: feedback on line exception class design
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: feedback on line exception class design
messages.body_plain:
I think we're on the same page as to the options.  Option 1 puts a policy requirement on almost all Stan code for exceptions to work (functions can only throw a limited set of exceptions).  Option 2 complicates catching behaviour a bit.

Personally, I think policy should only be added if absolutely necessary because it makes it more difficult for people to write new, correct code.  As such, I would argue for option 2.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Sun, Mar 8, 2015 at 6:37 PM Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
> > On Mar 9, 2015, at 4:57 AM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > The template pattern is really nice, but I'm not convinced it's worth it if you're not going to catch std::runtime_error and throw line_number_exception<std::runtime_error>.
>
> That is what I'm going to do, but I think the "not"
> in your sentence was a typo.
>
> > The reason is that the pattern suggests that you should be able to catch a line_number_exception<special_exception_type> but that's only going to work if the model catches special_exception_type  and rethrows appropriately.  I.E., reasonably expected behaviour from the pattern will not work as expected which seems like a bad idea.
>
> This is exactly what I was worried about, too.  The
> class works fine on its own and does as intended, but
> the way I was planning to use it in try/catch blocks will
> just catch std::exception (superclass of std::runtime_error)
> and throw line_number_exception<std::exception>.
>
> >
> > I see two possibilities:
> > 1. Identify a short list of the exceptions that our code can throw and catch and rethrow explicitly.  Make it a policy that any functions to be used in models can *only* throw those kinds of exceptions.
>
> If I do that, I can include long catch sequences and throw
> the right kind of exception.
>
> > 2. Make a generic model_exception class which derives from std::exception.  Provide all the convenient RTTI/polymorphism features as functions of model_exception for when people care about exactly which exception was thrown.  E.G., have a model_exception::is_runtime_error() and model_exception::get_runtime_error().  This is almost what you have right now in effect but without the convenience functions since people would have to catch line_number_exception<std::exception> and then use RTTI to do anything more sophisticated than get the error message and line number.
>
> That's more along the lines of what I was thinking, though
> rather than building that into the class, I'd just let users
> grab a reference to the std::exception and have at it themselves.
>
> Do you think it's worth building that in?  I tend to not want
> to build in generic functionality when it's accessible almost
> as easily externally.
>
> I could build it in generically with a pair of template
> functions:
>
>   template <typename T>
>   bool is<T>() { ... }
>
>   template <typename T>
>   const T& get<T>() { ... }
>
> ...
> > exec.cpp:19:20: error: no member named 'to_string' in namespace 'std'
> >             + std::to_string(line)
> >               ~~~~~^
> > 1 error generated.
> >
> > StackOverflow appears to have some hits on this.
> >
> > This appears to fix it
> >
> > //            + std::to_string(line)
> >             + static_cast<std::ostringstream*>( &(std::ostringstream() << line) )->str()
>
> I'd either just use a stringstream everywhere (as we
> do elsewhere to allow printing) or revert to C-style
> strtoi().  I think I'll go with the stringstream because
> it's a bit more C++-ey.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: best of both worlds for located exceptions?
messages.subject_clean: best of both worlds for located exceptions?
messages.body_plain:
Here's what I came up with.  It doesn't require any policy
on Stan code and will use RTTI to create an appropriately
typed exception (that is, catchable by the nested exception
type) if it's in the standard library (option 1), falling back
on std::exception for other types (option 2).

I've attached the code and the test to show how it works
on its own.  I also pushed to feature/issue-1195-runtime-error-lines
in case anyone wants to run the test.

My lingering uncertainty is whether it's safe to store the
nested type as a const reference and return it the same way
from the getter.  It'd be easy enough to copy the nested exception
and return it by value rather than by reference.  (One of the
current tests for reference equality will fail, though.)

My plan is to wrap the code blocks of all relevant functions
and the constructor as:

  int line__ = -1;
  try {
    ...run updating line number...
  } catch (const std::exception& e) {
    throw_located_exception(e,line__);
  }

If the exception e is an instance of any of the std library
exception types, the rethrown exception will be catchable
by its type E or by located_exception<E>.  I could add some
Boost types to the parade.

I also built in the inspection with RTTI for good measure
in case someone wants to just catch std::exception and use
RTTI to inspect the type of the nested exception and get it
dynamically cast to a given type.

I learned a lot about exceptions building this thing today!

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] plotting sampler parameters
messages.body_plain:
What you want is

(a) Average accept stat
(b) Histogram of treedepth (to check whether it’s saturating against max_depth)
(c) Number of iterations with n_divergent != 0.

Distributions of accept_stat (vs parameter values) can be sort of useful in some cases
but it’s hard to disentangle the meaning without really knowing the sampler.  Plotting it
vs iteration is just a bad proxy for plotting vs parameter value so I wouldn’t recommend it.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] best of both worlds for located exceptions?
messages.body_plain:
I read over the code quickly and two small things:

1. In located_exception::get() I think it should be a dynamic cast, not a static one.
2. In throw_located_exception() if it falls through to the std::exception case, it might be worth emitting a warning with the typeid of the exception that was thrown so that we know when this case gets hit.

Otherwise it looks great!

Cheers,
Marcus

On Mon, Mar 9, 2015 at 9:47 AM Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Fixed.  I'd actually implemented the fix function but
> hadn't plumbed it into the constructor.

> >
> >> On Mar 9, 2015, at 11:29 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> Still not compiling without -std=c++11
> >>
> >> goodrich@T540p:/tmp$ clang++-3.6 -fsyntax-only located_exception_test.cpp
> >> In file included from located_exception_test.cpp:1:
> >> ./located_exception.hpp:80:24: error: no member named 'to_string' in namespace 'std'
> >>                + std::to_string(line)
> >>                  ~~~~~^
> >>
> >> instead do
> >>
> >>            + static_cast<std::ostringstream*>( &(std::ostringstream() << line) )->str()
> >>
> >> Ben
> >>
> >>
> >> On Monday, March 9, 2015 at 1:50:17 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> Here's what I came up with.  It doesn't require any policy
> >> on Stan code and will use RTTI to create an appropriately
> >> typed exception (that is, catchable by the nested exception
> >> type) if it's in the standard library (option 1), falling back
> >> on std::exception for other types (option 2).
> >>
> >> I've attached the code and the test to show how it works
> >> on its own.  I also pushed to feature/issue-1195-runtime-error-lines
> >> in case anyone wants to run the test.
> >>
> >> My lingering uncertainty is whether it's safe to store the
> >> nested type as a const reference and return it the same way
> >> from the getter.  It'd be easy enough to copy the nested exception
> >> and return it by value rather than by reference.  (One of the
> >> current tests for reference equality will fail, though.)
> >>
> >> My plan is to wrap the code blocks of all relevant functions
> >> and the constructor as:
> >>
> >>  int line__ = -1;
> >>  try {
> >>    ...run updating line number...
> >>  } catch (const std::exception& e) {
> >>    throw_located_exception(e,line__);
> >>  }
> >>
> >> If the exception e is an instance of any of the std library
> >> exception types, the rethrown exception will be catchable
> >> by its type E or by located_exception<E>.  I could add some
> >> Boost types to the parade.
> >>
> >> I also built in the inspection with RTTI for good measure
> >> in case someone wants to just catch std::exception and use
> >> RTTI to inspect the type of the nested exception and get it
> >> dynamically cast to a given type.
> >>
> >> I learned a lot about exceptions building this thing today!
> >>
> >> - Bob

enough, but we may have to go back to trying this route.

On Tue, Mar 10, 2015 at 09:48:17AM +1100, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I should also add what my first mentor at SpeechWorks told me
> when I asked how version control could possibly work:
>
>   Merge before everyone else and then it's there problem!
>
> There is some wisdom in this:  smaller, shorter-lived branches
> are the way to go.

I think the way you permit/encourage free-wheeling merging is part of
the problem. Linear history created with more rebasing and limited
merging is much easier to understand than the dense web of merges that
appears in the stan repo.

A good reason to make a merge commit is if somebody else contributed the
changes and your role is only to merge them. You might merge your own
branch too if there is a sequence of commits that are related to the
same logical change.

In my opinion.

messages.subject: Re: log_prob [w/o dropping constants]
messages.body_plain:
If you want to do that, you need to replace every
statement of the form

  y ~ foo(theta);

with

  increment_log_prob(foo_log(y,theta));

The code generated for a program has a template parameter
propto__ on the log_prob function that if set to false will
keep everything --- we need to get that plumbed through
the calls to allow it as an option at the top level.

- Bob

Well, I thought you were opposed to proliferating variants on the same distribution name. But it would be good to create an idiom that was common across many of the distributions that are used for GLMs.

Hi Joshua,

I saw you made another comment regarding git history.

What's the value of following development history? Perhaps if we had an actual use case, we'd be more careful.

Avi

messages.subject_clean: help using foo(const MatrixBase<T>&) with (u * v)
messages.body_plain:
We're trying to follow the advice on this page:

  http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html

and running into trouble passing the expression template (u * v)
to a function declared as suggested above.

It seems to work fine for transpose, for Map, for MatrixXd, but
here's a minimal example of the problem we're running into with
products:

-------------------------------------------
#include <Eigen/Dense>

template <typename Derived>
double foo(const Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived>& a, int m, int n) {
  return a(m,n);
}

int main() {
  Eigen::MatrixXd u(2,2);
  u << 1, 2, 3, 4;

  Eigen::MatrixXd v(2,3);
  v << 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6;

  foo(u*v, 0, 0);

  return 0;
}
--------------------------------------------

~/temp2$ clang++ -I ~/stan/lib/eigen_3.2.2 eigen-test.cpp

~/temp2$ ./a.out
Assertion failed: (this->rows() == 1 && this->cols() == 1), function coeff, file /Users/carp/stan/lib/eigen_3.2.2/Eigen/src/Core/ProductBase.h, line 141.
Abort trap: 6

~/temp2$ clang++ --version
Apple LLVM version 6.0 (clang-600.0.56) (based on LLVM 3.5svn)
Target: x86_64-apple-darwin14.1.0
Thread model: posix

--------------------------------------------------------

Here's the relevant part of Eigen/src/Core/ProductBase.h:

    typename Base::CoeffReturnType coeff(Index row, Index col) const

I'm missing how this is relevant, because we're comparing

  foo(y,pair(a,b))

and

  foo(y,a,b)

We already overload to vectorize the distributions and operations
like multiply() are super-overloaded.

So I would suggest something like

  normal_lm(y, x, beta, sigma);

which would be equal to

  normal(y, x * beta, sigma);

But I think that only works for (matrix x, vector beta),
or were you imagining also having (row_vector x, vector beta)?

What would happen to the other arguments and vectorization?

> But it would be good to create an idiom that was common across many of the distributions that are used for GLMs.

OK, that's some motivation.  But then we'd need to
introduce pair() into the language to use it, right?  I probably
misunderstood what you were suggesting.

> We could also do Kronecker products this way and things like D * L. Basically anything where we want to represent multiplication but not actually multiply anything right away.
>
> And by "user", do you mean a client of the C++ API
> or an end user of RStan?
>
> Both
>
> And which doc are we talking about --- the API doc in
> doxygen?  We've been very inconsistent with that, but
> I'm trying to add proper doc to all my commits now.
>
> Actually, the API doc may have a higher read rate than the user manual.

I'd bet dollars to donuts that's not true.  Nobody ever sends
us corrections to the API doc!

That will be super helpful.  I like the layout, too.

Calling it lookup rather than stan_lookup may
be a problem with more namespace clashes.  Will we be able to do

I have no idea if anyone (including CRAN) will be testing hardware
other than Intel.

messages.body_plain:
The proximate cause here seems to be fvar's use of
boost::math::isnan() to set the tangent to NaN.  But
it would probably creep in elsewhere, because I don't see
why that one's special.  I was hoping we could just get rid
of the problem, which we may be able to do by not using
Boost's isnan anywhere.  I'm getting lost in all the refactoring,
but my understanding was that we were going to get rid of
Boost's isnan() and use our own.

Ben, if including this in var.hpp with no #ifdef

      var(__float128 x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }

lets you compile, can you try this:

#ifdef BOOST_MATH_USE_FLOAT128

      var(__float128 x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }
#endif

That may introduce an order dependency, and if it doesn't work,
maybe a spell-corrected version of my first attempt would work (I forgot
the final "__" on "__GNUC_MINOR__"):

#if (__GNUC__ > 4) || ((__GNUC__ == 4) && (__GNUC_MINOR__ >= 3))

      var(__float128 x) : vi_(new vari(static_cast<double>(x))) { }
#endif

That should not depend on Boost --- if we use the Boost property,
then we may have more ordering issues.

The offending bit of Boost code that enables the non-standard
type __float128 is here:

  lib/boost_1.55.0//boost/math/tools/config.hpp

which has:

#if defined(_GLIBCXX_USE_FLOAT128) && defined(BOOST_GCC) && !defined(__STRICT_ANSI__)
//
// Only enable this when the compiler really is GCC as clang and probably
// intel too don't support __float128 yet :-(
//
#  define BOOST_MATH_USE_FLOAT128
#endif

I'd go back to trying enable_if, but I couldn't get it to work on
Windows --- the tests all passed here and crashed and burned on Jenkins.

- Bob

Ah, you may misunderstand which part of history I am complaining about.
I am only complaining about the merges that say,

  Merge branch 'develop' of https://github.com/stan-dev/stan into develop

In my opinion, that should be a rebase. It is perfectly reasonable to
have parallel active branches under development and to merge them to
'develop' when they are ready. I am only complaining about merges in the
other direction.

More concretely, when you are getting ready to merge your branch, I
advocate,

  git fetch origin
  git rebase origin/develop

Instead of

  git pull origin

Or, I suppose you could do,

  git pull --rebase origin

but I find the 2 step fetch/rebase sequence easier to understand.

>    I'll wait for another screenshot to stand behind that last
>    statement.

messages.body_plain:
Ben --- do you want to chime in here?  I think you're
the one who knows the most about this.

I, for one, am happy to do whatever others think
best.  The merge bubbles are mildly annoying, but
I tend not to think of them.  I usually use git log
to look at history when doing the release notes.

I believe we discussed some way to mitigate the merge
bubbles way back when we were learning Git and decided
to keep them for reasons I don't remember and didn't
understand at the time.  Is it possible to get rid of
them by fast forwarding instead of rebasing and is that
safer?

I believe the danger of rebasing I was remembering was
about rebasing all the commits in a branch so that it
looked like a single commit when merged.  I'm also OK doing
that if there's no danger of losing work.  Very rarely,
if ever, are intermediate commits on branches worth saving.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebase?
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, Mar 12, 2015 at 09:55:51AM -0400, Daniel Lee wrote:
>    Joshua, quick question: if someone already did a:
>    git merge develop
>    how would they go about fixing that to look like a git rebase? Is that
>    easy to do?

Assuming your working tree is clean ('git status' shows nothing), then
you can do,

  git reset --hard HEAD^  # move your branch to the previous commit

The merge should be gone now and you can rebase at your leisure,

  git rebase develop   # or origin/develop

--

Daniel

I don't think there is an "easy" way. Certainly it can be done, but I
wouldn't urge you to go experiment unless you are confident in your GIT
skills. That said, you can rebase against develop even when there are
intervening merge commits. I haven't tried this recently, but I believe
those merges will disappear and may be replaced by empty commits or
commits with change fragments. Any fragments can be cleaned up with
interactive rebase. Various tutorials for interactive rebase are
available online, such as,

  http://andreabergia.com/git-rebase-interactive/

However, I will be entirely happy if merges from develop to topical
branches are created less frequently in the future. Changing the past is
often not worth the effort.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: rebase?
messages.body_plain:
Rebasing is fine if it's done on branches that haven't been pushed at all.  Once they've been pushed, they're public in a sense and other people can end up relying on their history.  Rebasing at this stage will break that history and require --force to push.  The issue really is that we often push our branches early.  Personally, I think this is good habit, as it backs up the branch.  It is also the most convenient way to share branches across multiple machines.  E.G., I use around three different machines for Stan development sometimes (office, laptop, server, etc).

One solution is to have a separate personal repository where no one can depend on your branch and you can break history at will.  Then, only when you're ready to merge and run testing, do you push the branch to the main Stan repo.  That said, I personally don't think it's worth the trouble for what is inherently a cosmetic issue.

Cheers,
Marcus

> skills. That said, you can rebase against develop even when there are
> intervening merge commits. I haven't tried this recently, but I believe
> those merges will disappear and may be replaced by empty commits or
> commits with change fragments. Any fragments can be cleaned up with
> interactive rebase. Various tutorials for interactive rebase are
> available online, such as,
>
>   http://andreabergia.com/git-rebase-interactive/
>
> However, I will be entirely happy if merges from develop to topical
> branches are created less frequently in the future. Changing the past is
> often not worth the effort.
>

messages.subject: Re: Polygamma
messages.body_plain:
Avi --- I just gave you post permission on stan-dev.  I thought we'd
done that already.  sorry.

As to the post content, we have trigamma plumbed all the way through
to the Stan language, so you can use it in models.  For which we have
to compute tetragamma and pentagamma (I didn't even know these had names)
for first and second-order derivatives of the trigamma.

Here's a nice reference for when they put tetragamma into MATLAB in 2002:

http://www.mathworks.com/company/newsletters/articles/the-tetragamma-function-and-numerical-craftsmanship.html

- Bob

> On Mar 13, 2015, at 3:16 AM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> There is this: <https://github.com/BoostGSoC13/boost.math/blob/master/boost/math/special_functions/polygamma.hpp>
>
> Otherwise, you can build the polygamma based on <http://dlmf.nist.gov/5.15>. I've built trigamma in VBA and I'm not even a programmer.
>
> Or, have I missed something so fundamental that I'm not even wrong? :)
>
> Avi

*****Begin Quote*****

Alternatively, we could revert to the previous toolchain, based on gcc 4.6.3. because I need to try it out in my own tests, and that means I need to
have it in hand by Wednesday, if I'm going to decide by Friday.  I will
not build this into Rtools before next Friday, so you'll need to
distribute this by some other means.
*****End Quote*****

Avi
