messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Sparse matrix-by-vector multiplication using available types
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, March 7, 2015 at 5:03:46 PM UTC-5, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> You could speed up the Stan version of the function by copying entries into two vectors and then calling dot_product().  This will get you almost as fast as would be possible if you implemented it in C++ and without the trouble.

I took your suggestion (Marcus) but instead of trying to do something complicated with the compressed-column version, I took the compressed row version which simplifies nicely into a dot product.  I'm going to try and figure out the testing framework (and work out any bugs) for this next but I would appreciate any comments.  I think this is the dot product version everyone was suggesting.

  /** Return the multiplication of the sparse matrix spefcified by
     * by values and indexing by the specified dense vector.
     *
     * The sparse matrix X of dimension m by n is represented by the

     * vector w (of values), the integer array v (containing one-based
     * column index of each value), the integer array u (containing
     * one-based indexes of where each row starts in w), and the
     * integer array z (containing the number of non-zero entries in
     * each row of w).

     *
     * @tparam T1 Type of sparse matrix entries.
     * @tparam T2 Type of dense vector entries.
     * @param m Rows in matrix.
     * @param n Columns in matrix.

     * @param v One-based column index of each value.
     * @param u one-based index of where each row starts in w.
     * @param z number of non-zero entries in each row of w.

     * @return dense vector for the product.
     * @throw ... explain error conditions briefly ...
     */
    template <typename T1, typename T2>

    inline

    Eigen::Matrix<typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1, T2>::type, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>

    sparse_multiply_csr(const int& m,
                    const int& n,
                    const Eigen::Matrix<T1, Eigen::Dynamic,1>& w,

                    const std::vector<int>& v,
                    const std::vector<int>& u,
                    const std::vector<int>& z,

                    const Eigen::Matrix<T2, Eigen::Dynamic,1>& b) {

      // a whole bunch of error checking goes here, e.g., m, n > 0,
      // etc. etc.  we can't throw index out of bounds exceptions at
      // run time

      typedef typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T1, T2>::type fun_scalar_t;
      Eigen::Matrix<fun_scalar_t, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>  y(m);

      Eigen::Matrix<T2,Eigen::Dynamic,1> b_sub(n);
      for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
        int end = u[i] + z[i] - 1;
        int p = 0;
        for (int q = u[i]-1; q < end; ++q) {
          b_sub(p) = b(v[q]);
          ++p;
        }
        y(i) = dot_product(w.segment(u[i]-1,z[i]),b_sub.segment(0,p-1));
      }
      return y;

    }

>
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus

>
>
>
> On Fri, Mar 6, 2015 at 7:20 PM Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I made a Stan function for sparse-matrix-by-dense-vector multiplication (appended below).  To use it you have to generate your matrix in compressed column format (one-indexed, since this is Stan-land) and pass the matrix as its dimensions (m, n), the values vector (w) and the three indexing arrays (v,u,z).  Memory-wise it's a win over using a big model matrix but speed-wise it's not much of a win unless I do gradients.  As a step towards that I'd like to implement it as a C++ function (and do the whole pull request thing if there's interest and I can figure out how to do the gradient).
>
>
>
> I couldn't sort out what the signature should be yet, so I put the Stan function into a placeholder model, got Stan to parse it to C++, and fixed things up from there.  I think I'm going on the right path here but I thought I'd ask for feedback to make sure I'm not completely off the rails.
>
>
>
> Thanks for any pointers,
>
>
>
> Krzysztof
>
>
>
>
>
> ---------------------- Stan sparse_multiply function
>
> // This function implements the multiplication of a sparse m by n
>
> // matrix, X, by the dense vector b.  The sparse matrix X is represented by a vector
>
> // of values and three indexing vectors which allow for fast sparse
>
> // matrix by dense vector multiplication.
>
> //
>
> // The matrix X is represented by the vector w (of values), the integer array v
>
> // (containing one-based row index of each value), the integer array u
>
> // (containing one-based indexes of where each column starts in w), and
>
> // the integer array z (containing the number of non-zero entries in
>
> // each column of w). The matrix dimensions, m and n are also passed.
>
> //
>
> // This outer loop runs over columns of the matrix X.  With the column
>
> // index in hand, The inner loop runs over the section of w and v for
>
> // each column.  The inner loop first calculates the row index 'i' for
>
> // each non-zero value in w, and then calculates how the associated non-zero
>
> // value from w is scaled by the approriate entry of b to contribute to the
>
> // appropriate entry of the output column vector.
>
> //
>
> // The function works by incrementing the entries of the entries of the
>
> // output vector, y, because the outer loop is iterating column-wise
>
> // over X.
>
>
>
>
>
> vector sparse_multiply (
>
>   int m, int n,
>
>   vector w, int[] v, int[] u, int[] z,
>
>   vector b
>
> ) {
>
>   vector[m] y;
>
>   y <- rep_vector(0.0,m);
>
>   for (j in 1:n) {
>
>     int i;
>
>     for (q in u[j]:(u[j]+z[j]-1)) {
>
>       i <- v[q];
>
>       y[i] <- y[i] + w[q] * b[j];
>
>     }
>
>   }
>
>   return y;
>
> }
>
>
>
>
>
> ----------------------- Edited from Stan-generated C++
>
> #ifndef STAN__MATH__MATRIX_FAKE_SPARSE_HPP
>
> #define STAN__MATH__MATRIX_FAKE_SPARSE_HPP
>
>
>
> #include <stan/math/matrix/Eigen.hpp>
>
> #include <vector>
>
>
>
> namespace stan {
>
>   namespace math {
>
>
>
>     template <typename T2__, typename T6__>
>
>     inline
>
>     Eigen::Matrix<typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T2__, T6__>::type, Eigen::Dynamic,1>
>
>     sparse_multiply(const int& m,
>
>                         const int& n,
>
>                         const Eigen::Matrix<T2__, Eigen::Dynamic,1>& w,
>
>                         const std::vector<int>& v,
>
>                         const std::vector<int>& u,
>
>                         const std::vector<int>& z,
>
>                         const Eigen::Matrix<T6__, Eigen::Dynamic,1>& b) {
>
>         typedef typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T2__, T6__>::type fun_scalar_t__;
>
>         {
>
>             Eigen::Matrix<fun_scalar_t__,Eigen::Dynamic,1>  y(m);
>
>             y = rep_vector(0.0,m);
>
>             for (int j = 1; j <= n; ++j) {
>
>                 {
>
>                     int i(0);
>
>                     (void) i;   // dummy to suppress unused var warning
>
>                     for (int q = u[j-1]; q <= (u[j-1] + z[j-1] - 1); ++q) {
>
>                         i = v[q-1];
>
>                         y[i-1] += w[q-1] * b[j-1];
>
>                     }
>
>                 }
>
>             }
>
>             return stan::math::promote_scalar<fun_scalar_t__>(y);
>
>         }
>
>     }
>
>   }
>
> }
>
>
>
> #endif
>
>
>
>
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
[posting to stan-dev]

I don't have permission to write to eigen --- can you
thank them for us Daniel?  They've told us what we need
to do.

The Eigen devs are super helpful, as always.  It's clear
to me what's going on and why they did it, and both Christoph
and Gael's messages say the same thing and make it clear how
we should write the code.  To summarize, from Gael's message:

Instead of what we were trying, bar(u * v), he suggested:

> If you really want to evaluate the product coefficient-wise, then call:
>
> bar(u.lazyProduct(v))
>
> lazyProduct returns a "true" expression template.
>
> if you are going to access to all coefficients then rather call bar like this:
>
> bar((u*v).eval()).

I was hoping we'd be able to just pass the expression template through,
but apparently not.  On the other hand, we do have to .eval() at
some point.

I agree that their page on writing functions did not make
it clear that products were special expression templates
in Eigen 3.  But it makes sense --- they can efficiently
calculate all the coeffs in a matrix product, but if you
call it elementwise, it's going to be hugely inefficient.
Michael and I are discussing some of the implications for autodiff
around the autodiff paper, and that discussion should probably
be imported into stan-dev --- bottom line is that using their
matrix ops without any specialized gradients produces code on
the order of 100 times faster than the naive loops for
(100x100) Matrix<var> * Matrix<var> products (lots of 100s there).

- Bob

> On Mar 14, 2015, at 7:57 AM, Gael Guennebaud <gael.gu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> as Christoph said evaluating matrix product coefficient-wise is highly inefficient, therefore in Eigen 3 we decided to forbid coefficient accesses to product expression unless this a inner product. This is what the assertion exactly does.
>
> The following:
>
> bar((u*v).transpose())
>
> works because (u*v) gets evaluated into a MatrixXd temporary by the Transpose expression.
>
> If you really want to evaluate the product coefficient-wise, then call:
>
> bar(u.lazyProduct(v))
>
> lazyProduct returns a "true" expression template.
>
> if you are going to access to all coefficients then rather call bar like this:
>
> bar((u*v).eval()).
>
>
> gael
>
>
>
> On Fri, Mar 13, 2015 at 3:57 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> Hi Christoph,
>
> Thank you for the response. I think the access within the function masked the real problem we are having.
>
> The issue: matrix multiplication does not behave like other expression templates, e.g. transpose, Map.
>
> I am following instructions here: http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html
>
> Example function (bar.hpp):
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> #include <Eigen/Dense>
> #include <iostream>
>
> template <typename Derived>
> void bar(const Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived>& a) {
>   std::cout << "a(0): " << a(0) << std::endl;
> }
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
>
>
> Example that works:
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> #include "bar.hpp"
>
> int main() {
>   Eigen::MatrixXd u(1,1);
>   u << 1;
>   Eigen::MatrixXd v(1,2);
>   v << 1, 2;
>
>   bar((u*v).transpose());
>   bar((u*v).transpose().transpose());
>
>   return 0;
> }
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
>
>
>
> Example that does not work, but I expect to work:
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> #include "bar.hpp"
>
> int main() {
>   Eigen::MatrixXd u(1,1);
>   u << 1;
>   Eigen::MatrixXd v(1,2);
>   v << 1, 2;
>
>   bar(u*v);
>
>   return 0;
> }
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>

messages.body_plain:
Robert:

Thanks!  We would very much like to have a Stata interface
for Stan.

Would you mind working in GitHub on stan-dev?  If so, we should
set up a GitHub repo, such as

  stan-dev/statastan

or however you want to name it.  I guessed it'd be spell corrected
to "statistician", but Google disagrees:

  Did you mean: statesman  statscan  statisten  status tan

We also need a name, such as

  StataStan

or however you want to name it.   Then we can list it on our home page.

It would also need an explicit license if we're going to redistribute.
I strongly prefer the most liberal (in the sense of fewer restrictions,
not most "left") license compatible with Stata.

We can give you (Robert Grant) push permission on the repo and either
take the project over from you to manage or let you manage it.

Our dev process is here:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki

including tips for using GitHub.  Before you panic, we've been much laxer in
enforcing the process outside of stan-dev/stan and stan-dev/cmdstan.

- Bob

Daniel

> I added 1) the extractors required to test sparse multiplication, 2) some simple tests for those extractors, 3) some simple tests for the sparse multiplication, and cleaned it up.  The whole thing is at:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/compare/feature/sparse_multiply
>
> In the testing doc when it says "we want to make sure all tests get tickled and the appropriate exception types are thrown and documented", it's not clear to me what Stan-appropriate behavior is.  I'm throwing in some context below and asking for clarification.
>
> In multiply_test I see:
>
> TEST(MathMatrix,multiply_m_v_exception) {
>  stan::math::matrix_d m;
>  stan::math::vector_d v;
>
>  m.resize(3, 5);
>  v.resize(5);
>  EXPECT_NO_THROW(stan::math::multiply(m, v));
>
>  m.resize(3, 0);
>  v.resize(0);
>  EXPECT_THROW(stan::math::multiply(m, v),
>               std::invalid_argument);
>
>  m.resize(2, 3);
>  v.resize(2);
>  EXPECT_THROW(stan::math::multiply(m, v), std::invalid_argument);
> }
>
> So with wrong-size arguments, I should be throwing std::invalid_argument directly or doing something with the code in stan::math::check_*?  Not sure which way to go.

Use the built-in check functions and if the ones you need
aren't available, write more.

> It looks like the rest of the testing is helping people not shoot themselves in the foot (and devs figure out future breakage)... I'm ok completing it if I can get some direction on what to do.  I guess I can also generate some matrices and compare sparse_multiply results to the dense multiply(X,b).

You can look at some of our other functions for guidance.

The general point of doc and testing is complementary.  The
doc should define all the constraints (e.g., what sizes things have to
be relative to each other), and the tests should test they are
handled appropriately.

The tests should also check boundary conditions, such as if a size
zero matrix or vector is allowed, then it should behave properly.

> In the mean time I think this works as intended and I'll see what some test models do with it.  Thanks to everyone for getting this sorted out so far!

Great.

messages.subject: C++ API stability & backward compatiblity
messages.body_plain:
This is something I'd like to discuss at the next Stan
meeting if Daniel and Michael will be around.

As is, with our habit of reorganizing the C++ code
every few releases, I have to agree with Ben that an external
developer has no reason to trust us to not break backward
compatiblity in any given release --- our major release numbers
are meaningless at the C+ API level.

This is not only an issue for external developers, but
also ones working on branches within stan-dev/stan, as
well as RStan and PyStan.  I'm pretty much having to rely
on grep now to find anything with the latest reorganization.
I'd strongly prefer this not to be a permanent state.

Daniel:  Is there a time when we can declare pencils down
on all the refactoring of the math library?  Is the plan still
to pull it out into its own repo?  Maybe that's when we
should plan to advertise more stability and we should discourage
anyone from using the API until then.

- Bob

- std::string to_json()  (since PyStan and RStan need a way of knowing about the values that are set)

think we treat the C++ api as in a development state for now.

If you want me to put a line in the sand, I'd say end of June. That'll
give us two months after Bob gets back to hash out whatever final
details we need to consider before we freeze the API.

>  Is the plan still

from the rest of Stan. I think we encourage people to use the API when
we get the paper out detailing how to use it.

Anyone else have any thoughts?

messages.subject: Re: LDLT v LLT for cholesky decompose
messages.subject_clean: LDLT v LLT for cholesky decompose
messages.body_plain:
LDLT in Eigen is not so good for Stan, except for checking positive definiteness and solving systems of equations. Eigen does pivoting so it is really a

Sigma = PLDL'P'

decomposition. Also, the pivoting is discontinuous, so it is not great for HMC.

Ben

>
> Rob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: LDLT v LLT for cholesky decompose
messages.body_plain:
We could, in the future, have a decomposition that returned P * L and D. But I think we should leave cholesky_decompose as is because it returns an actual lower-triangular matrix. All these matrix decompositions have analytic derivatives, but they are really tedious. The first-order derivatives of LDLT involve inverses of principal submatrices of the original matrix.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The problem is that stan::math only applies to primitives (double
and int, for Stan).  Rather than calling functions with explicit
namespaces, you need to have a using statement so that
argument-dependent lookup can do its magic:

   using stan::math::dot_product;
   ...
    y(i) = dot_product(w_sub,b_sub);

Just make sure the autodiff versions of functions you need
are included --- they should be for a real model.

- Bob

P.S.  See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument-dependent_name_lookup

P.P.S.  If you want to see a real error novel, try mucking about with
        the lazy evaluation expression templates in the parser :-)

messages.subject: shinyBS breaks shinyStan (fixed, kind of)
messages.body_plain:
If you know anyone who recently installed shinyStan and is having issues with the customization/options panels please point them to the troubleshooting page of the shinyStan repo on GitHub. I just updated it with a temporary fix for the following really frustrating problem:

The author of the shinyBS package (one of the packages shinyStan depends on) made a bunch of small changes directly in what had been the stable branch of shinyBS on GitHub instead of testing those changes in feature and bugfix branches. Of course one of those changes (or several of them, I'm not sure yet) seems to cause some serious problems for shinyStan including 1) preventing some of the collapsible panels from opening and closing properly and 2) changing the background and text colors for those collapsible panels that do open in such a way that the text isn't really visible anymore.

Of course he also doesn't really use pull requests so I had to comb through his commit history until I found the most recent one that doesn't cause these issues. I still need to go through his changes in detail to figure out exactly what's causing the problem, but for the time being I've changed the install_shinystan.R file in the shinyStan develop branch so that it installs shinyBS using that commit I found as the git reference.

Unfortunately anyone who installed shinyStan between last week and a few hours ago when I changed the install_shinystan file would have also installed the new changes to shinyBS and so shinyStan probably isn't fully functional for them (although they might just think it's designed poorly).

Anyway, to avoid these problems going forward I'm seriously considering severing ties (so to speak) with shinyBS for future versions of shinyStan, but it would require writing a ton of extra code.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Stan Autodiff/Math Library Name
messages.body_plain:
As much as I like Aki's suggestion, I like simple, as in:

  StanMath

though camel case has perhaps seen better days, so
maybe

  The Stan Math Library

In particular, I would rather reinforce than split the
Stan brand.  I find the Sacado (autodiff) as part of
Trilinos (larger math lib) thing really confusing.

If Andrew insists on throwing SEO and branding to the
wind, and we have to go with a name, we could use "Mike"
in the spirit of "Stan" --- it was the code name of
the first hydrogen bomb test and also a riff on Michael :-)
Or Edward after Teller if we want to full nuclear, or maybe
Nicholas after Metropolis (though it's the piece w/o
Metropolis!)

Now that Betancourt's in London, maybe he can nip down to
the East End for some help with some Cockney rhyming slang,
which is easiest to explain with an example:

  Water Closet -> Waterloo -> loo

>From Wikipedia:

  One example is replacing the word "stairs" with the rhyming
  phrase "apples and pears". Following the pattern of omission,
  "and pears" is dropped, thus the spoken phrase "I'm going up the
  apples" means "I'm going up the stairs".

- Bob

messages.subject: interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
I think one way to take the burden off the interfaces
checking consistency of commands is to break the monolithic
command-line call down into multiple little function calls.
In that situation, almost everything will be consistent.

R goes partway down this path, but not all the way, because
the stan() function still encompasses both NUTS and HMC.

For example, if the commands were

* stan_sample_nuts(...)
* stan_sample_hmc(...)
* stan_optimize_lbfgs(...)
* stan_optimize_bfgs(...)

(The names aren't important, so please don't get hung up here if
you think they should say "bayes" or "mcmc" or "(p)mle" or "map"
or "mode" or whatever.)

Then almost all of the built-in options will be legal.  To work
this out in more detail for nuts, here are all the config options
(including model, which is implicit in CmdStan):

nuts(model (file | string | dynamic-object),
     max_depth (int > 0),
     metric (unit | diag |dense),
     stepsize (double > 0),
     stepsize_jitter (double in (0,1)),
     num_samples (int >= 0),
     num_warmup (int >= 0),
     save_warmup (bool),
     thin (int >= 1),
     adapt(false | true
           | dictionary(gamma (double in ?),
                       delta (double in (0,1)),
                       kappa (double in ?),
                       t0 (double in ?)),
     data (var_dictionary),
     init (double > 0 | var_dictionary),
     seed (int in (0,2^32 - 1)),
     output_file (file),
     diagnostic_file (file),
     refresh (int >= 0) );

That's it.  Now if within Python or R, you have some simple
routines to validate ranges and validate the various values, you'd
be good to go without any complicated config construction or
callbacks.  These routines could be used across the different
functions.

This doesn't specify defaults, but presumably that's also easy.

Adaptation is worth special attention, because it's
a big disjunction that's either boolean with defaults or
specifies overrides in terms of a nested argument.

The huge advantage is that the error messages will match what
the names are in RStan or PyStan.

I'm not sure if allowing the disjunctive types, like init
is a good idea in R or Python.  If you have two different
arguments, then there are consistency requirements, so I'd
rather see that as a substructure, just as in CmdStan.

Then, to run, there needs to be a way to turn these
into a config C++ object that can actually be passed to
the Stan C++ to do the work, but that shouldn't be that
hard, either.

I'd like to compare how much work this would be to
marshaling a config object from a similar input in a dictionary,
converting to JSON, sending it to Stan C++ for validation,
then interpreting the results back in terms of the actual
argument names in PyStan or RStan.

This seems way more modular to me and doesn't require
any kind of config within Stan C++ --- it all becomes
a C++ structure that just runs and then CmdStan would get
all the config stuff that's currently in Stan C++.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
With N observations and K predictors, the data matrix
will be (N x K) and the parameter vector (K x 1) in
a simple non-multilevel regression, then you get N
dot products, each involving K multiplications and K
additions (assuming you start with zero).

The naive approach introduces (2 * K * N) nodes into the
expression graph, each taking a node pointer (8 bytes),
vtable pointer (8 bytes), value (8 bytes), adjoint (8 bytes),
and two operands (16 bytes), for a total of (96 * K * N)
bytes of storage.

The dot-product approach introduces N nodes, each taking
a node pointer (8 bytes), vtable pointer (8 points),
value (8 bytes), and  2*K operands, for a total of
((24 + 2K) * N) bytes of storage.  The overall fraction
of memory used is:

   (24 + 2 * K) / (96 * K)

K=1:   26 / 96
K=10:  44 / 960
K=100: 224 / 9600

The naive approach requires (2 * K * N) virtual function
lookups and the dot-product approach only N.  The overall
arithmetic operations are the same each way.

I think I did that arithmetic right.

- Bob

I looked at your branch:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/compare/feature/sparse_multiply

and the first problem is that you didn't follow our convention
of naming branching after the issues.  No big deal, but it
makes them hard to put together later.  I know it's verbose.
We should probably remove the "issue-" convention.

I didn't understand the difference between _csr and _csc.
The final "r" vs. "c" seems to hint at some row vs. column
difference, but the doc seemed to be identical and I couldn't
easily work through the code.

It would be tricky to have the _csr version use dot product.
You'd need to accumulate two vectors of unknown size to start,
so it'd require two passes or using something like a vector
to accumulate.

Some other comments.

You don't want to do this:

  Eigen::Matrix<T1,Eigen::Dynamic,1> w_sub;
  w_sub = w.segment(u[i]-1,z[i]);

but rather just do the compound decleare/define:

  Eigen::Matrix<T1,Eigen::Dynamic,1> w_sub
    = w.segment(u[i]-1,z[i]);

or even just apply the copy constructor directly as in:

  Eigen::Matrix<T1,Eigen::Dynamic,1> w_sub(w.segment(u[i]-1,z[i]));

For this function, and others like it:

  template <typename _Scalar>
  const std::vector<int>
  extract_u(Eigen::SparseMatrix<_Scalar, Eigen::RowMajor> A) {
    std::vector<int> u(A.outerSize()+1);
    for ( int j = 0; j <= A.outerSize(); ++j)

      u[j] = *(A.outerIndexPtr()+j) + 1;  // make 1-indexed
    return u;
  }

1.  no reason to use _Scalar for type, just use Scalar, or
even just T.

2.  No space between "(" and "int"

3.  Spaces around "+".

4.  Stay away from pointer manipulation.  I don't know how
the sparse matrices work in Eigen, but presumably there's some
way to get at the values you want other than pointer ops.

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/group__TutorialSparse.html

I didn't even see outerIndexPtr() in their tutorial and the
API doc says it's just there for compatibility with other
libs.  That means you might be able to just construct the
vector you want with iterators.

5.  I didn't understand the make 1-indexed comment, but then
these functions are tricky and I didn't spend much time trying
to figure it out.

- Bob

Thanks for taking a peek.

The extractors _are_ the same, for some reason I couldn't get the compiler to
do the right thing without having a second set for Eigen::RowMajor...
I'll have to take
another shot at it sometime now that everything works.

The multiplication is different because csc (that's what they call it...) is by
column and csr is by row.  The doc looks the same until you realize
that column/row
switch places between the two... sorry there seems to be no good way of
documenting this. Eigen documents it in one place and pretends people
have sed in their brain.

>
> It would be tricky to have the _csr version use dot product.
> You'd need to accumulate two vectors of unknown size to start,
> so it'd require two passes or using something like a vector
> to accumulate.

Agreed (well, for the csc version, csr does use dot product). Can't
see how that would be efficient.

>

>

>
> or even just apply the copy constructor directly as in:
>

That's what I did but compilation failed so I split it out.  I'll go
back and figure out
if your suggestions do work, maybe I was doing something weird the
first time around.

>   const std::vector<int>
>   extract_u(Eigen::SparseMatrix<_Scalar, Eigen::RowMajor> A) {

>     for ( int j = 0; j <= A.outerSize(); ++j)
>       u[j] = *(A.outerIndexPtr()+j) + 1;  // make 1-indexed

>   }
>
> 1.  no reason to use _Scalar for type, just use Scalar, or
> even just T.
>
> 2.  No space between "(" and "int"
>
> 3.  Spaces around "+".

ok.

>

> the sparse matrices work in Eigen, but presumably there's some
> way to get at the values you want other than pointer ops.

I looked for that first, but there seriously seems to be no good way
of getting at it.  There's a high-level
API, and then there's pointers...

>

Yeah, it's really screwy since the function is exposed in Stan so indexing is
supposed to start at one, but it's doing pointer arithmetic so obviously starts
at zero... the up side is that the test I have written uses these
functions to do
multiplication with a dense X in sparse format so all the indexing is exercised.
That part I'm confident about.  The check_ functions I call catch most
of the ways
you can screw things up (they mirror the doc).  If you generate a
screwy 'z' vector you can still
get an out-of-bounds index (whatever that error's called...) but that's why I
exposed the extractors through rstan... I suppose I could check that one
during multiplication.

There's a lot not to like about the whole thing....

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
Surprise!  I fundamentally disagree.

The problem with splitting up the API into a bunch of small functions
is that we have no way to enforcing a consistent user experience
which will force users to learn each interface separately.  We’re
already seeing this in RStan which is rapidly drifting from CmdStan
(and hence JuliaStan and MatlabStan) and taking PyStan with it.
It’s already a pain in the ass to do these workshops where I have to
relearn all of the idiosyncrasies of each interface in addition to all
of the usual work.

Then there’s the problem of actually implementing an interface,
which would now require the implementer to come up with a user
experience and piece together all of the modular components.

I am very much in favor of having a monolithic API route that
provides at least a marginal enforcement of a unified user
experience.  Interfaces will always be able to screw it up with
enough work but the path of least resistance will be a similar
user experience everywhere.

On Mar 18, 2015, at 4:39 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I think one way to take the burden off the interfaces
> checking consistency of commands is to break the monolithic
> command-line call down into multiple little function calls.
> In that situation, almost everything will be consistent.
>
> R goes partway down this path, but not all the way, because
> the stan() function still encompasses both NUTS and HMC.
>
> For example, if the commands were
>
> * stan_sample_nuts(...)
> * stan_sample_hmc(...)
> * stan_optimize_lbfgs(...)
> * stan_optimize_bfgs(...)
>
> (The names aren't important, so please don't get hung up here if
> you think they should say "bayes" or "mcmc" or "(p)mle" or "map"
> or "mode" or whatever.)
>
> Then almost all of the built-in options will be legal.  To work
> this out in more detail for nuts, here are all the config options
> (including model, which is implicit in CmdStan):
>
> nuts(model (file | string | dynamic-object),
>     max_depth (int > 0),
>     metric (unit | diag |dense),
>     stepsize (double > 0),
>     stepsize_jitter (double in (0,1)),
>     num_samples (int >= 0),
>     num_warmup (int >= 0),
>     save_warmup (bool),
>     thin (int >= 1),
>     adapt(false | true
>           | dictionary(gamma (double in ?),
>                       delta (double in (0,1)),
>                       kappa (double in ?),
>                       t0 (double in ?)),
>     data (var_dictionary),
>     init (double > 0 | var_dictionary),
>     seed (int in (0,2^32 - 1)),
>     output_file (file),
>     diagnostic_file (file),
>     refresh (int >= 0) );
>
> That's it.  Now if within Python or R, you have some simple
> routines to validate ranges and validate the various values, you'd
> be good to go without any complicated config construction or
> callbacks.  These routines could be used across the different
> functions.
>
> This doesn't specify defaults, but presumably that's also easy.
>
> Adaptation is worth special attention, because it's
> a big disjunction that's either boolean with defaults or
> specifies overrides in terms of a nested argument.
>
> The huge advantage is that the error messages will match what
> the names are in RStan or PyStan.
>
> I'm not sure if allowing the disjunctive types, like init
> is a good idea in R or Python.  If you have two different
> arguments, then there are consistency requirements, so I'd
> rather see that as a substructure, just as in CmdStan.
>
> Then, to run, there needs to be a way to turn these
> into a config C++ object that can actually be passed to
> the Stan C++ to do the work, but that shouldn't be that
> hard, either.
>
> I'd like to compare how much work this would be to
> marshaling a config object from a similar input in a dictionary,
> converting to JSON, sending it to Stan C++ for validation,
> then interpreting the results back in terms of the actual
> argument names in PyStan or RStan.
>
> This seems way more modular to me and doesn't require
> any kind of config within Stan C++ --- it all becomes
> a C++ structure that just runs and then CmdStan would get
> all the config stuff that's currently in Stan C++.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>
>
>

> The problem with splitting up the API into a bunch of small functions

This is the key to the disagreement, and I disagree very
strongly.

I think the experience from R should be R-like, from
Python should be Pythonic (can't believe I just said that),
and from the command line, should be shellish.

The only way to make everything literally the same would be to have
the R user experience look like this:

> stan_make("foo.stan");

> foo("sample algorithm=hmc metric=unit_e engine=nuts max_depth=15 data file=model.data.R init=modelinit.R random seed=5 output file=samples.csv");

> stan_print("samples.csv")

No way of doing extract, no way of calling log prob directly,
no way of passing inits in as a function, no way of passing data
in as list, no plotting, etc.  Basically nothing's that not
built into CmdStan.

I guess we could use list notation to make it a bit more R-like,
without straying too far from the command line you set up:

> foo(list("sample", algorithm=list("hmc",metric="unit_e", engine=list("nuts", max_depth=15), data=list(file="model.data.R"), init="model.init.R",random=list(seed="5")...);

Is this what you are envisioning?  If not, would you mind elaborating
a bit on what you think the R user experience should be?

> which will force users to learn each interface separately.

I don't think many users are going to learn multiple Stan
interfaces, so I think that's a moot point other than for us,
as you note in the next paragraph.

>  We’re
> already seeing this in RStan which is rapidly drifting from CmdStan
> (and hence JuliaStan and MatlabStan) and taking PyStan with it.
> It’s already a pain in the ass to do these workshops where I have to
> relearn all of the idiosyncrasies of each interface in addition to all
> of the usual work.

CmdStan only?  I'm doing one next week exclusively in RStan.
Then I believe Andrew, Daniel, and I will be doing a three-day
course using just RStan.

> Then there’s the problem of actually implementing an interface,

This is a separate issue.

To clarify, I'm *not* still advocating a modular approach on
the R side where we expose samplers, etc.  You and Daniel
convinced me that would be too hard to maintain.

What I'm suggesting is having the interface provide an idiomatic
way of piecing together a C++ structure (including
writers, iostreams, etc.) that would be passed to Stan C++
and further validated on that side to make sure nothing untoward
happens.

Then no holds barred once the data gets back on the interface
side.

You'll never be able to agree with Andrew as to what the
default print should look like.  You'll be stuck on scientific
notation before even getting going.

> which would now require the implementer to come up with a user
> experience and piece together all of the modular components.

Back to the first disagreement.  I think that's a good thing!
Otherwise, we wind up with every interface looking like the
command line and being heavily limited in what it offers.

> I am very much in favor of having a monolithic API route that
> provides at least a marginal enforcement of a unified user
> experience.  Interfaces will always be able to screw it up with
> enough work but the path of least resistance will be a similar
> user experience everywhere.

Could you please sketch out what you think the R user experience
would look like so as to match the one in CmdStan?  Or Python's?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
I think there's a great deal everyone agrees on. Splitting up the
interface into smaller functions sounds good to me, but perhaps that can
be tabled until Stan 3.0 and the proposed reorganization of
RStan/PyStan.

As for the general question of how to provide parameters, I think
there's probably some middle ground we can reach.  Those using Stan know
they are getting into a DSL, so we have *some* freedom to depart from
Pythonic and R styles. We already all agree, for example, that the
parameters should have the same names (i.e., "adapt_t0" and not
"adapt.t0"). I think we can make other small concessions here in order
to have an experience that is as consistent as possible. I want
switching between R and Python to be as painless as possible.)

I think there are two important things that the Stan C++ services
library should provide:

- Validation of config (e.g., is adapt_int_buffer positive)
- One source of truth about default values.

While promoting code reuse is the proximate goal, just having
RStan/PyStan and CmdStan on the same page about something as modest as
config validation would probably do more in the short term to move us
towards a consistent user experience than anything else I can think of.

Best,

Allen

On 03/18, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Adaptation is worth special attention, because it's
> a big disjunction that's either boolean with defaults or
> specifies overrides in terms of a nested argument.
>
> The huge advantage is that the error messages will match what
> the names are in RStan or PyStan.
>
> I'm not sure if allowing the disjunctive types, like init
> is a good idea in R or Python.  If you have two different
> arguments, then there are consistency requirements, so I'd
> rather see that as a substructure, just as in CmdStan.
>
> Then, to run, there needs to be a way to turn these
> into a config C++ object that can actually be passed to
> the Stan C++ to do the work, but that shouldn't be that
> hard, either.
>
> I'd like to compare how much work this would be to
> marshaling a config object from a similar input in a dictionary,
> converting to JSON, sending it to Stan C++ for validation,
> then interpreting the results back in terms of the actual
> argument names in PyStan or RStan.
>

This sounds good to me (serializing/deserializing a C++ object). I'd
still like to consider Protocol Buffers here instead of JSON here
because PB is/are fast (I think we could even put initial values and
data in there) and there's the explicit schema that everyone can read
(which JSON would lack). Moreover, you can specify some consistency
requirements in Protocol Buffers explicitly (see Union Types,
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/techniques#union).
Clearly Python and R will need to know something about what a valid
config looks like -- but I'd prefer that they need not have to know too
much.

As for passing large amounts of data via Protocol Buffers, there's this
magical-sounding "ZeroCopy" functionality provided by PB that sounds
pretty good
(https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.io.zero_copy_stream#ZeroCopyInputStream).

Best,

-a

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
Let me be more particular about what I mean:

The C++ code needs a few things from each interface
in order to be executed — a configuration, from where
certain info will be obtained (data, initialization, etc),
and from where certain info will be written (info, errors,
output, diagnostics, etc).

The interfaces can implement these however they want,
so for example CmdStan can grab inputs from files
where as RStan and PyStan can grab them from the
local environment (making the experience appropriate
to their respective environments).  Same with the outputs.
The implementations vary but the basic interaction is
the same.

Where our disagreements lie is with the configuration.
Firstly, I want every interface to run the same optimization,
sampling, and diagnostic routines so that a user can
switch interfaces and have the same functionality —
I don’t see how this is guaranteed without enforcing
a monolithic function.

Secondly, I want _every_  configuration option available
from each interface so it’s just as easy to, say, tweak the
step size in RStan as it is in CmdStan (the “control”
interface makes me sad every time I have to get in there).
Again, how the configuration is constructed can vary

The first part we agree on. The second part, enforcing a monolithic
function, is where I disagree. The point was to have the interfaces
implement a few interfaces and that gets passed into a function.

I'm ok with the idea of having a config that's parsed, but I think we
need to separate out the configuration for the algorithms vs the
configuration that's needed to handle implementation of these things
that need to be passed in.

exposed doubles instead, right?

> If we just give the interfaces a mess of routes and let
> them do what they want I don’t see how we can guarantee
> any uniformity of experience across the interfaces.

I'm not suggesting that. I'm suggesting that there are lots of smaller
functions and there's a single large function that RStan, PyStan, and
CmdStan share. But, I can already imagine CmdStan wanting to build an
executable that only includes NUTS or only includes optimization.

>   stepsize_jitter (double in (0,1)),
>   num_samples (int >= 0),
>   num_warmup (int >= 0),
>   save_warmup (bool),
>   thin (int >= 1),
>   adapt(false | true
>         | dictionary(gamma (double in ?),
>                     delta (double in (0,1)),
>                     kappa (double in ?),
>                     t0 (double in ?)),
>   data (var_dictionary),
>   init (double > 0 | var_dictionary),
>   seed (int in (0,2^32 - 1)),
>   output_file (file),
>   diagnostic_file (file),
>   refresh (int >= 0) );
>
> That's it.  Now if within Python or R, you have some simple
> routines to validate ranges and validate the various values, you'd
> be good to go without any complicated config construction or
> callbacks.  These routines could be used across the different
> functions.
>
> This doesn't specify defaults, but presumably that's also easy.
>
> Adaptation is worth special attention, because it's
> a big disjunction that's either boolean with defaults or
> specifies overrides in terms of a nested argument.
>
> The huge advantage is that the error messages will match what
> the names are in RStan or PyStan.
>
> I'm not sure if allowing the disjunctive types, like init
> is a good idea in R or Python.  If you have two different
> arguments, then there are consistency requirements, so I'd
> rather see that as a substructure, just as in CmdStan.
>
> Then, to run, there needs to be a way to turn these
> into a config C++ object that can actually be passed to
> the Stan C++ to do the work, but that shouldn't be that
> hard, either.
>
> I'd like to compare how much work this would be to
> marshaling a config object from a similar input in a dictionary,
> converting to JSON, sending it to Stan C++ for validation,
> then interpreting the results back in terms of the actual
> argument names in PyStan or RStan.
>
> This seems way more modular to me and doesn't require
> any kind of config within Stan C++ --- it all becomes
> a C++ structure that just runs and then CmdStan would get
> all the config stuff that's currently in Stan C++.
>
> - Bob

functions but if you want to be an official Stan interface then
you have to use the big interface function that wraps all of
them up into a singular user experience.

messages.subject: missing data (vs. parameters) in BUGS/JAGS
messages.body_plain:
What does BUGS/JAGS do if you have missing non-modeled
parameters.  That is, if I have a regression and have
missing predictors, but no distribution given to the predictors.

For example, what if I have the model

  sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5)
  beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5)
  alpha ~ cauchy(0,2.5)
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ normal(alpha + beta * x, sigma)

and pass in data where some of the x are NA?
It'd gripe and fail to run, right?  At least that's what
I hope it would do.

That is, BUGS/JAGS don't handle missing data per se,
only missing parameters, using Andrew's definitions of
parameter vs. data from BDA 1:1.

- Bob

Krzysztof:

I completely agree that hte names of arguments should be
consistent, even if "_" isn't as idiomatic in R as "." as
a separator.

I do not want to build a typical R function, just one that
uses data types that are familiar from R, such as lists,
etc., and that returns output in the form usable in R, such
as a reference object.

Allen and Michael:

I'm not sure how to do that in a transparent way without
having the glue:

  R command
  -> C++ config object
  -> Stan C++ validator
  -> Stan C++ optimization, sampling, or validation
  -> C++ result object

Michael:

Do you object to all the additional functions inside R,
like extract() and what not?  Or do you object to the
what Ben's calling "andrewfy", which was formerly referred
to by Andrew as "Sebastian's function"?  That is, something
that provides make-like behavior inside the stan() call?
Or are you insisting on a separate make() then run call?
I'm OK with the latter, but RStan's going down the former
path.

What we really need is a spec from you as to what RStan
and PyStan interfaces would look like.  I lack the imagination
to envsion what you're talking about other than what I put
in the previous message.  Is the lack of a counter-proposal
implicit acknowledgment that what I wrote is what you'd like
to see in RStan?

What kind of drift are you talking about specifically?

More below.

> On Mar 19, 2015, at 1:18 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> I'm ok with the idea of having a config that's parsed, but I think we

>> Sure, but it's even more uniform if there was a small function that
>> exposed doubles instead, right?
>
> Example?

I think the main issue here is whether the config is

  * a string wrapping up the command-line interface,
  * a structured protocol buffer
    - with data
    - without data
  * a C++ object

I've been arguing for the C++ object approach, but Allen thinks
it's complicated to do that from PyStan (for reasons I don't
undersetand enough about Python to understand).

Whatever we do, CmdStan is going to make a call to make to
build the model (either wrapped up in another function, or
expicitly called as make as the CmdStan manual suggests now).
Whatever else we do, RStan and PyStan are going to need an
R and Python function to call respectively.

Is it really that hard to validate input from the interfaces?
There's almost no consistency issues from a lower-level interface
standpoint (that is, once you specify

  method=sample algorithm=hmc engine=nuts

The one thing that would be nice for the C++ structure or
protocol buffers that Allen brought up is consistent
unions (aka variant data types).  There's a nice
implementation in Boost that uses only static types, but it's a
bit of a pain to use because every function has to be defined
via callbacks.  And there's the compile-time hit because of all
the templates.

>> I'm not suggesting that. I'm suggesting that there are lots of smaller
>> functions and there's a single large function that RStan, PyStan, and
>> CmdStan share. But, I can already imagine CmdStan wanting to build an
>> executable that only includes NUTS or only includes optimization.
>
> I agree that command should be split up into smaller functions
> for easier testing (that part is already happening — which should
> make it easier to test each function and also make it easier to
> create tests that require running the algorithms, such as the
> statistical validation tests) but I still think that the single large
> function should be the only official “route” exposed to the
> interfaces.

What I really dislike about this is the fact that it has
a polymorphic return.  You get one set of output from optimize
and a different one from validate and a third one from
optimize.

I dislike even more the R idiom of just defining a massive
structure and partially populating it on return.  Especially
the way it's used in something like glm to be mutable without
enforcing consistency.

> In other words, the Stan C++ API would expose all the little
> functions but if you want to be an official Stan interface then
> you have to use the big interface function that wraps all of
> them up into a singular user experience.

If we do this (and I don't like it), then I agree that
we'd want to have the interfaces pass in a giant string.

Michael --- you still haven't said what you want that function
to look like from the RStan or PyStan side.  Until we have
an example of that, it's hard to talk about whether it's acceptable
to R/Python users or not.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> I'm not sure how to do that in a transparent way without
> having the glue:
>
>  R command
>  -> C++ config object
>  -> Stan C++ validator
>  -> Stan C++ optimization, sampling, or validation
>  -> C++ result object

Wouldn’t the second and third steps be wrapped together?
As in you construct a config object, pass it into the Stan
call, and then get back your results.

> Do you object to all the additional functions inside R,
> like extract() and what not?  Or do you object to the
> what Ben's calling "andrewfy", which was formerly referred
> to by Andrew as "Sebastian's function"?  That is, something
> that provides make-like behavior inside the stan() call?
> Or are you insisting on a separate make() then run call?
> I'm OK with the latter, but RStan's going down the former
> path.
>
> What we really need is a spec from you as to what RStan
> and PyStan interfaces would look like.  I lack the imagination
> to envsion what you're talking about other than what I put
> in the previous message.  Is the lack of a counter-proposal
> implicit acknowledgment that what I wrote is what you'd like
> to see in RStan?

If we wanted to be _really_ consistent amongst the interfaces
then the UX would be something like

1) Preprocessing
2) Compile Stan object/executable
3) Configure algorithm arguments and callbacks
4) Call Stan object/executable with configuration, returning results in fit object
5) Postprocessing

(1) and (5) are left to the interfaces so we don’t have to worry about those.
Each interface can add whatever functionality it wants here, such as print
and fit, although it would be great to unity these as much as possible.

(2) and (4) is a bit tricky because right now RStan and PyStan try to wrap
these together which necessitates tricks like Sebastian’s function.  Personally
I’d much rather have the user create an explicit object and then call a run method
of that object, so if you want to rerun without recompiling you just call the
method again instead of creating a new object (this also parallels the CmdStan
procedure).

(4) is also completed in RStan and PyStan because the results aren’t
uniformly accessible.  Instead you have to access the samples
and the sampler parameters separately in incredibly annoying ways,
but this is just a disagreement about exactly what extract should return.

My big complaint is in (3) which is where some of the biggest disparities
are (i.e. that awkward control list).  The config can be implemented by
each interface separately but the user should have access to the
arguments in roughly the same way — for example, if we maintain the
current hierarchical structure then there should be some way of
specifying the config hierarchically.  The flattened single arguments of
RStan and PyStan upsets me.

> What kind of drift are you talking about specifically?

In terms of time-dependence I’m specifically referring to all of these
functions that try to wrap RStan functionality into a UX that’s moving
further and further away from how the other interfaces are implemented.

> having the glue:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] interfaces and command error-checking (Rstan/PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, March 19, 2015 at 5:26:09 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> (2) and (4) is a bit tricky because right now RStan and PyStan try to wrap
> these together which necessitates tricks like Sebastian’s function.  Personally
> I’d much rather have the user create an explicit object and then call a run method
> of that object, so if you want to rerun without recompiling you just call the
> method again instead of creating a new object (this also parallels the CmdStan
> procedure).

The stan() function does (2), (3), and (4) together but it is possible to do them separately. Or technically, you can do (2) separately but (3) and (4) are lumped together. In any event, if necessary, we could change that. We could even use more Pythonic calling semantics

model <- stan_model("foo.stan")
model$config(adapt_delta = 0.9)
model$sampling()
model$summary()

The only difficulty is that such idioms are relatively new to the R language and people (especially Andrew) are not used to them. It isn't a technical problem. I do mostly agree with Bob that the interfaces should behave more like the external software, although in this case it would be more a case of RStan behaving more like R will a few years in the future.

> My big complaint is in (3) which is where some of the biggest disparities
> are (i.e. that awkward control list).  The config can be implemented by
> each interface separately but the user should have access to the
> arguments in roughly the same way — for example, if we maintain the
> current hierarchical structure then there should be some way of
> specifying the config hierarchically.  The flattened single arguments of
> RStan and PyStan upsets me.

That is not inherent either. Lots of R functions take a flat control list but we could specify that in a hierarchical fashion with either a list of lists or a JSON thing. Almost no one would even notice if we changed it completely.

RStan could adapt to almost anything and I think PyStan could as well. We just need to come to an agreement on monolithic config vs. modular and JSON vs. Protocol Buffers and things like that.

Ben

messages.subject: Comments on Command Refactor
messages.body_plain:
If people have a minute can you check out the current progress at
feature/issue-1361-writer_callback?  This branch introduces a
writer callback and then refactors a ton of services to use the
callback.  Some of that refactoring addresses a bunch of
outstanding issues and substantially pushes command towards
the spec outlined at https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-API-Refactor.

If people are cool with it I’ll proceed to the next step, which involves
pushing the writer callback all the way through the sampling and
optimization codes and then updating an incredibly large number of
tests (not to mention adding a bunch of new ones).

-Betancourt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Comments on Command Refactor
messages.body_plain:
I did some major edits on the services and interface proposal:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Stan-API-Refactor

I tried to flesh out the missing arguments to the command
service function, added a discussion of templating vs.
abstract base classes for the callback option, and added
a discussion of just replacing everything with JSON or
Protocol Buffers.  I tried to lay out more of what each
component needs as well as discussing some pros and cons
as I see them without trying to editorialize my own opinions.

My own opinion is that we should go the callback route.
I think the pros outweigh the cons, unless the pain to
Allen and Jiqiang of writing C++ is so great as to outweigh
the other benefits.

Feel free to continue editing --- I'm sure I missed some of
the pros and cons.

We need to dive one level deeper and start fleshing out what
each of the elements is going to be.  I think I'll go and drop
in the CmdStan config skeletons, which I think show what's going
on.

This also brings up the issue of whether the interfaces provide
a monolithic god-object for config and single function, or whether they
break things down more modularly.  I'm in favor of smaller functions,
which is why I documented CmdStan as I did, whereas I believe Michael's
in favor of the god-object approach, which is why the config is
implemented as it is.  So the implementation/interface decisions
can go their own way.

- Bob
